slides.definition:
Passive income is a way to earn regular, consistent money without actively working to gain it. It's not free money — it's made through hard work up front so you can build stability for years to come. Unearned income is different: money you receive without effort, like gifts or random payments. That is not the same as passive income.

Examples: creating and selling an online course, renting out property.

pros.title: No active labor forever
pros.description: Sometimes earned after an up-front investment — sometimes built from work you already did.

slides.title: Passive vs Unearned
slides.leftBody: Built once — or set up with real work up front — then it can earn repeatedly over time. Think royalties, a course that keeps selling, or rent after the heavy lifting is done.
slides.rightBody: Random or gifted money that isn't pay for a job right now — birthday cash, some prizes, surprise refunds, or money someone gives you just because.
slides.footer: Both can land in your pocket; passive usually comes from systems you built, while unearned often shows up without an ongoing 'clock-in' job.

slides.definition:
Interest income will likely be your first form of consistent passive-style income. Your money earns more by sitting in the right account, and the bank (or government, for some bonds) pays you an extra percentage each year for letting them use it.

Examples: high-yield savings, bank accounts, bonds.

pros.title: Super easy

slides.definition:
Money you earn from owning stocks or index funds/ETFs — through dividends (regular cash payouts) and capital gains (profit when you sell higher than you bought). If some of these words don't make sense right now, don't worry — they'll all be covered in due time.

Examples: Quarterly dividend checks, selling a stock for a profit, ETFs, or occasionally interest from bonds (basically a loan to a company).

slides.title: Pros and Cons of Portfolio Income

pros.title: Versatility
pros.description: You can actively invest and turn it into a career, or passively invest and have it be a truly passive source of income on the side.

pros.title: Growth over time
pros.description: Investing in an index fund or ETF spreads risk across many holdings — many people use them to ride long-term market growth, though nothing is guaranteed.

cons.title: Investing takes homework
cons.description: Dumping money into a random stock is a great way to go broke. You need to research, learn, and understand how markets work before you dive in.

slides.question: You own 10 shares of a company and get $8 every quarter just for holding. What kind of income is this?
options: Business Income
Active Income
Portfolio Income
explanations: Not quite. We'll talk about it in the next slide!
Nope. Portfolio income can happen without you needing to do a thing after the initial investment.
That's right! This is what a dividend is.

slides.definition:
You create or own a system that generates money with little to no ongoing effort from you. Once the setup is complete, the income continues whether you're working or not. This can have the potential to be life-changing wealth.

Examples: Selling goods or products, providing services, other people's subscriptions.

slides.title: Pros and Cons of Business Income

pros.title: Extremely high income potential
pros.description: Starting a business can be much more lucrative than working a job.

pros.title: You call the shots
pros.description: You own your business — you can run it the way you think is best.

cons.title: Highest upfront effort
cons.description: Starting a business or working your way to real traction is no easy task.

cons.title: Financial risk
cons.description: Starting a business doesn't mean you'll become Steve Jobs — there's no guarantee of success.

options: Portfolio Income
Active Income
Business Income
explanations: ❌ This is tied to a channel you built — not mainly stocks or funds.
❌ Not anymore. Since you've stopped uploading, this isn't active income from ongoing work.
✅ Exactly! You built a system that keeps paying you.

Getting dividends + interest + business checks while you sleep, while ALSO still being able to work if you want. (All 5 Buckets)

Stacking dividends, interest, and business income — while still keeping active income as an option — is how many people build real flexibility. All it takes is dedication and a willingness to learn.

slides.detailText: Self-employment means you work for yourself — not a company. This lesson covers how self-employment income works, what makes it different from a traditional job, and the tax realities you need to know.

slides.question: What does self-employment mean?
options: Working for a company
Running your own work and being your own boss
Earning passive income
explanations: That's traditional employment — you have a W-2 employer.
Exactly. When you're self-employed, you set your own hours, find your own clients, and are responsible for your own income.
Passive income can be part of self-employment, but they're not the same thing.

slides.definition:
When you work for a company as an employee, they handle your taxes for you — automatically withholding federal, state, and Social Security taxes from every paycheck.

At the end of the year they give you a W-2 form, which summarizes what you earned and what was withheld.

When you're self-employed or do freelance / contract work, clients pay you the full amount — no taxes withheld. At the end of the year they may send you a 1099 form, but either way the IRS expects you to report and pay taxes on every dollar you earned.

This includes side hustles, freelancing, and gig apps.

slides.title: W-2 vs. 1099 at a Glance
slides.leftBody: Employer withholds taxes from every paycheck. You get a W-2 form each January. Taxes are partially handled for you.
slides.rightBody: You receive the full payment — no withholding. You owe taxes yourself and must track them all year. You're responsible for every dollar.
slides.footer: Most self-employed people and freelancers are 1099 workers. More freedom, but more responsibility.

habits: Spending every dollar you earn without setting taxes aside
whyBadExplanations: When you're self-employed, the IRS didn't withhold anything — so the tax bill comes all at once. A common rule of thumb is to set aside 25–30% of every payment you receive so you're never caught off guard at tax time.

pros.title: Freedom and flexibility
pros.description: You set your own hours, choose your clients, and work from wherever makes sense.

pros.title: Higher earning potential
pros.description: Without an employer taking a cut, your hourly rate can be much higher than a regular job.

cons.title: Taxes are harder
cons.description: No employer to help — you track income, pay quarterly estimated taxes, and file a more complex return.

cons.title: Unstable income
cons.description: Some months are great; others are slow. Budgeting without a predictable paycheck takes discipline.

slides.prompt: If you started freelancing tomorrow, what's one thing you'd want to charge for? And what percentage would you set aside for taxes each time you got paid?

slides.title: Lesson 2.5 Takeaways
slides.subline: Self-employment gives you freedom — but responsibility comes with it.
takeaways: Self-employed = you are your own boss
W-2: employer handles taxes. 1099: you handle taxes.

slides.definition:
The process of creating something — a product, service, or system — that solves a problem or meets a need, and then building it into an ongoing source of income.

Entrepreneurs aren't just 'business owners.' They're people who see gaps between what exists and what could exist — and take action to close that gap.

slides.title: 4 Signals of a Real Business Idea

items.title: Solves a Problem
items.description: People pay when you fix a real pain point — not just a nice-to-have.

items.title: Repeat Demand
items.description: Customers come back. One-time sales are fine; recurring revenue is better.

items.title: Profitable
items.description: Revenue consistently exceeds your costs — what's left is yours to keep.

items.title: Scalable
items.description: Can grow without you doing proportionally more work each time it grows.

pros.title: Extremely high upside
pros.description: A successful business can generate far more income than any single salary.

pros.title: You're in control
pros.description: You own the decisions — the direction, the culture, and the vision are all yours.

cons.title: High upfront effort
cons.description: Building something real takes time, energy, and often money before anything comes back.

cons.title: Real financial risk
cons.description: Many businesses don't succeed. There's no guarantee, and some people lose money.

slides.myth: You need a million-dollar idea to be an entrepreneur.
slides.truth: Most successful businesses start by solving a small, specific problem really well. A lawn mowing service, a tutoring business, or a simple Etsy shop are all entrepreneurship — and all three can grow into something real.

slides.prompt: What's one problem you notice in your everyday life — something that's annoying, slow, or just done badly — that you could imagine solving for people?

slides.title: Lesson 2.6 Takeaways
slides.subline: Entrepreneurship is about solving problems — start small, stay consistent.
takeaways: Entrepreneurship = creating value others will pay for
Look for problems with repeat demand that can turn a profit
The upside is huge — but so is the risk and effort required
You don't need a massive idea to start

name: Jobs vs. Careers
description: A job and a career are two different things — but one often leads to the other. This lesson breaks down the difference, why both matter, and how to think about your own path.
objectives: Understand the difference between a job and a career
Recognize how jobs can build toward a career over time
Avoid the myth that jobs are useless or that careers are automatic

slides.title: Jobs vs. Careers
slides.subtitle: Unit 2 · Lesson 7
slides.detailText: A job and a career are two different things — but one often leads to the other. This lesson breaks down the difference, why both matter, and how to think about your own path.

objectives: Understand the difference between a job and a career
Recognize how jobs can build toward a career over time
Avoid the myth that jobs are useless or that careers are automatic

slides.definition:
A job is typically short-term, task-based work done in exchange for pay. You show up, do the work, get paid, and move on.

A career is a long-term professional path — built over years through skills, experience, relationships, and deliberate choices. Most careers are made up of multiple jobs.

slides.title: Job vs. Career
slides.leftBody: Immediate income. Short-term. Task-driven. Often interchangeable with other similar roles.
slides.rightBody: Long-term growth path. Built through accumulated experience. Direction matters as much as the day-to-day work.
slides.footer: A job gets you paid today. A career shapes where you're headed over years.

slides.title: It's the summer before your junior year. What do you do?
slides.optionA: Take any job for quick cash — mowing lawns, fast food, retail
slides.optionB: Intern at a local business in a field you're curious about
slides.consequenceA: Smart move — quick cash is real and useful, and even 'basic' jobs teach time management, reliability, and customer skills. Nothing wrong here.
slides.consequenceB: Less immediate pay, but you gain industry exposure, references, and a head start on a career path. Valuable if you already have direction.

slides.question: Which of these is true about jobs and careers?
options: Jobs are useless — they don't lead anywhere
A career is just a fancy word for a long job
Jobs build the experience, skills, and connections that make careers possible
explanations: False. Even 'basic' jobs teach reliability, communication, and work ethic — skills that transfer everywhere.
Not quite. A career is a deliberate path built over time, not just duration.
Exactly. Very few people land their dream career without a string of jobs that built them up to it.

slides.title: How Jobs Become a Career
steps: Get a job — any job that teaches responsibility
Develop skills and build a track record
Make connections and ask good questions
Move toward roles aligned with your longer-term direction
slides.subtitle: Most careers look messy in the middle — that's normal.

slides.prompt: Think of a job you'd actually take right now — even if it seems small. What skills could it teach you? Could it connect to any longer-term direction you're interested in?

slides.title: Lesson 2.7 Takeaways
slides.subline: Jobs and careers aren't opposites — they're stages.
takeaways: Job = short-term, income-focused work
Career = long-term path built from experience and intention
Every job teaches something — treat them that way
Jobs build the skills and connections that make careers happen

name: Hourly vs. Salary
description: When you start working, you'll get paid in one of two ways: by the hour, or a fixed salary. This lesson breaks down how each works, what the tradeoffs are, and how to evaluate a job offer beyond just the number.
objectives: Understand the difference between hourly and salary pay
Know which type of pay can fluctuate and why
Weigh pros and cons of each pay structure
Learn to evaluate total compensation, not just the hourly rate or salary

slides.title: Hourly vs. Salary
slides.subtitle: Unit 2 · Lesson 8
slides.detailText: When you start working, you'll get paid in one of two ways: by the hour, or a fixed salary. This lesson breaks down how each works, what the tradeoffs are, and how to evaluate a job offer beyond just the number.

objectives: Understand the difference between hourly and salary pay
Know which type of pay can fluctuate and why
Weigh pros and cons of each pay structure
Learn to evaluate total compensation, not just the hourly rate or salary

slides.definition:
You earn a set amount for every hour you work. Work more hours, earn more money — but cut your hours and your paycheck shrinks.

Most entry-level and part-time jobs are hourly. In the U.S., hourly workers over 40 hours a week usually qualify for overtime pay (1.5× their rate).

You earn a fixed amount per year, divided into regular paychecks — regardless of how many hours you actually worked.

Salary is common in professional or office roles. A $52,000/year salary pays about $1,000/week before taxes — whether you worked 40 hours or 55.

slides.question: Which type of pay can change from paycheck to paycheck?
options: Salary
Hourly
explanations: Salary is the same every period — that's the point. It's predictable.
Right! If you work different hours each week, your hourly pay changes too. Sick day? Less money. Extra shift? More money.

pros.title: Hourly: Flexible earnings
pros.description: Pick up extra shifts to earn more. Overtime can pay well.

pros.title: Salary: Predictable income
pros.description: Same amount every paycheck — easier to budget and plan around.

cons.title: Hourly: Inconsistent pay
cons.description: Fewer hours = less money. Slow weeks can strain your budget.

cons.title: Salary: Hours can creep up
cons.description: No overtime — if your employer expects 55-hour weeks, you're working them for free.

slides.quote: The salary is just one number. Look at the full picture — benefits, paid time off, growth potential, and how many hours you're actually expected to work.
slides.author: Smart job evaluation

slides.prompt: If you had two job offers — one at $18/hour (hourly) and one at $38,000/year (salary) — what questions would you ask before deciding which pays better?

slides.title: Lesson 2.8 Takeaways
slides.subline: Don't just look at the number — look at the full package.
takeaways: Hourly = paid per hour worked; pay can vary week to week
Salary = fixed annual income split into regular paychecks
Hourly offers flexibility; salary offers predictability
Always evaluate total compensation, not just the base number

name: Minimum Wage and Worker Rights
description: Before you take your first job, you need to know your rights. This lesson covers minimum wage, what protections exist for workers, and how to handle it when something goes wrong.
objectives: Understand what minimum wage is and why it exists
Know your basic rights as a teen worker
Recognize when something is wrong on your paycheck and what to do about it

slides.title: Minimum Wage and Worker Rights
slides.subtitle: Unit 2 · Lesson 9
slides.detailText: Before you take your first job, you need to know your rights. This lesson covers minimum wage, what protections exist for workers, and how to handle it when something goes wrong.

objectives: Understand what minimum wage is and why it exists
Know your basic rights as a teen worker
Recognize when something is wrong on your paycheck and what to do about it

slides.definition:
The lowest hourly rate an employer is legally allowed to pay you. Federal minimum wage sets a floor, but many states and cities set their own higher minimums — your employer must pay whichever is higher.

As a teen worker, you're covered by these laws just like any adult employee.

slides.question: Why should teen workers care about their rights?
options: Only adults need to worry about worker rights
Rights directly affect your pay, your safety, and your working conditions
Knowing your rights lets you legally skip work whenever you want
explanations: Wrong — worker protections apply to you the moment you're employed, regardless of age.
Exactly. If you don't know your rights, you can't enforce them — and some employers (intentionally or not) won't remind you.
Not how it works! Rights protect you from unfair treatment, not from showing up.

slides.title: Your Basic Rights as a Worker

items.title: Fair Pay
items.description: You must be paid at least minimum wage for every hour worked, on time.

items.title: Legal Hours
items.description: Teen labor laws limit how many hours you can work, especially on school nights.

items.title: Safe Workplace
items.description: Your employer must provide a safe environment — hazardous conditions are illegal.

items.title: Accurate Records
items.description: You're entitled to records of your hours and pay. Keep your own records too.

habits: Not checking your paycheck when it arrives
whyBadExplanations: Paycheck errors happen — sometimes by mistake, sometimes not. If you never check, you'll never catch them. Always verify your hours, your rate, and the total match what you expected.

slides.scenario: You worked 20 hours this week but your paycheck only covers 17 hours.
slides.question: What's the right move?
options: Ignore it — it's probably fine
Check your own records, then politely ask your manager to review it
Quit on the spot
explanations: Never ignore a short paycheck. You earned that money and have a legal right to it.
Exactly. Keep your own log of hours so you can back yourself up — then raise it calmly with your manager or HR.
Quitting before addressing it means you may lose both the money and the job. Handle it first.

slides.prompt: Have you (or someone you know) ever been paid less than expected? What happened? What would you do differently now?

slides.title: Lesson 2.9 Takeaways
slides.subline: You can't protect what you don't know you have.
takeaways: Minimum wage is a legal floor — employers can't go below it
Teen workers have real rights: fair pay, safe conditions, legal hours
Always track your own hours — don't rely solely on your employer
If your paycheck is wrong, document it and address it directly

name: How to Read a Pay Stub
description: Your first paycheck can be confusing — the number is always less than you expected. This lesson teaches you what gross pay, net pay, and deductions mean so your paycheck never catches you off guard again.
objectives: Define gross pay, net pay, and deductions
Understand why your take-home pay is lower than your gross earnings
Know how to read a basic pay stub and spot errors

slides.title: How to Read a Pay Stub
slides.subtitle: Unit 2 · Lesson 10
slides.detailText: Your first paycheck can be confusing — the number is always less than you expected. This lesson teaches you what gross pay, net pay, and deductions mean so your paycheck never catches you off guard again.

objectives: Define gross pay, net pay, and deductions
Understand why your take-home pay is lower than your gross earnings
Know how to read a basic pay stub and spot errors

slides.term: Gross Pay, Net Pay, and Deductions
slides.definition:
Your pay stub has three key numbers:

• Gross Pay — what you earned before anything is removed
• Deductions — amounts taken out (taxes, insurance, etc.)
• Net Pay — what actually lands in your account (gross minus deductions)

Net pay is your real take-home money.

slides.question: Your gross pay is $500 and deductions are $90. What's your net pay?
explanations: That would be adding deductions — you subtract them.
That's gross pay — deductions haven't been removed yet.
Correct! $500 − $90 = $410. That's your take-home.
That's just the deduction amount — not your net pay.

slides.definition:
Amounts removed from your gross pay before you get it. Common deductions include:

• Federal and state income tax
• Social Security and Medicare (FICA)
• Health insurance premiums (if your employer offers it)
• 401(k) contributions (if you opt in)

Some deductions are mandatory; some are optional.

slides.scenario: You worked 15 hours at $14/hour — you expected $210. Your check says $171.
slides.question: Why is it lower than you expected?
options: Your boss stole from you
Deductions for taxes were taken out automatically
The bank made a mistake
explanations: Probably not — a ~$39 difference on $210 is typical for tax withholding. Check the stub before assuming the worst.
Correct. Federal tax, state tax, and FICA all come out automatically. This is totally normal — your gross was $210 but deductions brought your net to $171.
Your paycheck goes from your employer, not the bank — the bank just holds what your employer deposits.

slides.title: How to Review Every Paycheck
items: Check your hours match what you actually worked
Verify the hourly rate (or salary amount) is correct
Review each deduction line — does it match what you expected?
Confirm net pay = gross pay minus all listed deductions
Keep a copy (physical or photo) for your records

slides.prompt: Have you received a paycheck yet? If so — did you check it? If not — what's one thing you'd look for based on what you just learned?

slides.title: Lesson 2.10 Takeaways
slides.subline: Net pay is what you actually take home — plan your budget around that number.
takeaways: Gross = what you earned before deductions
Deductions = taxes and other removals (mandatory and optional)
Net = your actual take-home pay
Always check your stub — errors happen

name: Employee Benefits
description: Your paycheck is only part of what a job pays you. Benefits — health insurance, paid time off, retirement contributions — can be worth thousands of dollars and should factor into every job decision you make.
objectives: Understand what employee benefits are and why they matter
Identify the most common benefits and their real value
Learn to evaluate total compensation, not just salary

slides.title: Employee Benefits
slides.subtitle: Unit 2 · Lesson 11
slides.detailText: Your paycheck is only part of what a job pays you. Benefits — health insurance, paid time off, retirement contributions — can be worth thousands of dollars and should factor into every job decision you make.

objectives: Understand what employee benefits are and why they matter
Identify the most common benefits and their real value
Learn to evaluate total compensation, not just salary

slides.definition:
Compensation beyond your paycheck that your employer provides. Benefits are part of your total compensation package — and for many jobs, they can add tens of thousands of dollars of value on top of your base salary.

Never evaluate a job offer by salary alone.

items.title: Health Insurance
items.description: Employer-sponsored medical, dental, and vision — can save you thousands per year vs. buying it yourself.

items.title: PTO / Paid Time Off
items.description: Vacation days, sick days, and personal days you still get paid for. Valuable and often negotiable.

items.title: Retirement Match
items.description: Many employers match your 401(k) contributions — free money you should almost always take.

items.title: Education & Growth
items.description: Tuition reimbursement, training stipends, or certification funding can be worth thousands annually.

slides.title: Which job offer would you take?
slides.optionA: Job A: $55,000 salary, no benefits
slides.optionB: Job B: $48,000 salary + full health coverage, 3% 401(k) match, 15 PTO days
slides.consequenceA: Higher number on paper — but health insurance alone can cost $400–$600/month out of pocket, and you'd miss out on free retirement money. Net value may be lower.
slides.consequenceB: Lower base salary, but benefits could easily add $12,000–$15,000 in real value annually. Total compensation is often higher than it looks.

slides.myth: Benefits are just a bonus — the salary is what actually matters.
slides.truth: For many people, benefits represent 20–40% of their total compensation. Health insurance, retirement matching, and PTO have real dollar values. Always calculate the full package.

slides.prompt: If you had to choose between a job that pays $5,000 more but has no benefits, and one that pays less but includes full health insurance and a retirement match — what would you want to know before deciding?

slides.title: Lesson 2.11 Takeaways
slides.subline: Total compensation is salary + benefits — evaluate the full picture.
takeaways: Benefits are part of your pay — not just a perk
Health insurance, PTO, and 401(k) match have major dollar value
A lower salary with strong benefits can beat a higher salary without them
Always compare total compensation packages, not just base pay

name: Education and Experience
description: College is one path — not the only one. This lesson breaks down the real tradeoffs between degrees, trade programs, certifications, and hands-on experience so you can make an informed decision for your future.
objectives: Understand that multiple valid paths exist beyond a four-year college degree
Apply ROI thinking to education decisions — compare cost vs. earning potential
Identify which path aligns best with your goals and financial situation

slides.title: Education and Experience
slides.subtitle: Unit 2 · Lesson 12
slides.detailText: College is one path — not the only one. This lesson breaks down the real tradeoffs between degrees, trade programs, certifications, and hands-on experience so you can make an informed decision for your future.

objectives: Understand that multiple valid paths exist beyond a four-year college degree
Apply ROI thinking to education decisions — compare cost vs. earning potential
Identify which path aligns best with your goals and financial situation

slides.question: Which statement is true about education and career paths?
options: College is always the best path for everyone
Work experience is useless compared to a degree
There are multiple valid paths — the best one depends on your goals
You should never spend money on education
explanations: Not always true. College is great for some careers but a poor investment for others — it depends on the field and cost.
False. Many employers value demonstrated skills and real-world experience as much as (or more than) credentials.
Exactly. There's no one-size-fits-all answer — your field, goals, and financial situation all matter.
Education can be one of the best investments you make — the key is choosing wisely and understanding the return.

slides.definition:
ROI compares what you put in vs. what you get back. In education, it means asking: how much does this cost (tuition, time, debt) vs. how much more will I earn because of it?

A degree that costs $120,000 and leads to a $45,000/year job is a very different investment than one that costs $30,000 and leads to a $90,000/year job.

items.title: 4-Year College
items.description: Traditional degree path. High earning potential in many fields — but often high cost and debt. ROI varies enormously by major and school.

items.title: Trade Programs
items.description: Plumbers, electricians, HVAC techs, and welders often earn $60–$100k+. Programs take 1–2 years vs. 4, with far less debt.

items.title: Certifications
items.description: Short, focused credentials (coding bootcamps, Google certs, CompTIA, etc.) that are increasingly recognized by employers — often completed in months.

items.title: Hands-On Experience
items.description: Internships, apprenticeships, and entry-level jobs build real skills. Many people land careers through demonstrated work rather than credentials.

slides.myth: Without a college degree, you can't have a successful career.
slides.truth: Electricians, plumbers, and skilled tradespeople regularly out-earn college graduates with less debt. Tech, entrepreneurship, and many creative fields reward skills and portfolio over diplomas. The right path depends on the career — not a blanket rule.

slides.prompt: Think about a career you're curious about. What path — college, trade, certification, or experience — makes the most sense to get there? What would the cost and payoff look like?

slides.title: Lesson 2.12 Takeaways
slides.subline: The best path is the one with the best ROI for your specific goals.
takeaways: College is one path — not the only valid one
ROI means comparing education cost to your actual earning boost
Trades, certs, and experience are legitimate and often lucrative
Research the specific career you want before committing to any path

name: Skill Building and Networking
description: Skills get you in the door. Relationships open doors that don't even exist yet. This lesson covers which skills matter most early in your career and how to build a network that works for you — without it feeling fake or forced.
objectives: Understand what networking actually is (and isn't)
Identify the key skills that matter across nearly every career
Learn how to start building your network before you need it

slides.title: Skill Building and Networking
slides.subtitle: Unit 2 · Lesson 13
slides.detailText: Skills get you in the door. Relationships open doors that don't even exist yet. This lesson covers which skills matter most early in your career and how to build a network that works for you — without it feeling fake or forced.

objectives: Understand what networking actually is (and isn't)
Identify the key skills that matter across nearly every career
Learn how to start building your network before you need it

slides.definition:
Skills are the abilities you build through practice and learning. Networking is the deliberate process of meeting and building real relationships with people in fields you care about.

Together, they create opportunity: skills prove what you can do, and your network connects you to the people who have the roles worth doing.

slides.question: What is networking?
options: Using people to get what you want
Building genuine, mutually beneficial relationships over time
Just adding people on LinkedIn
explanations: That's the wrong framing — transactional networking tends to backfire. Real networking is about giving, not just taking.
Exactly. Good networking is about being genuinely curious, adding value, and staying in touch. It pays back over years, not overnight.
LinkedIn is a tool, not a strategy. Adding connections without real interaction doesn't build a network.

items.title: Communication
items.description: Writing clearly, speaking confidently, and listening well — the skills every employer lists first.

items.title: Organization
items.description: Showing up on time, meeting deadlines, and managing your own work without being managed.

items.title: Digital Literacy
items.description: Spreadsheets, email, video calls, basic data tools — expected everywhere, not just tech jobs.

items.title: Professionalism
items.description: How you show up matters: your reliability, tone, attitude, and willingness to take feedback.

slides.title: How to Start Networking as a Teen
steps: Start with people you already know — teachers, coaches, family friends
Be genuinely curious — ask about their work and how they got there
Follow up when you say you will, and thank people who help you
Build your presence online (LinkedIn, portfolio site) before you need it
Keep showing up — relationships compound over time
slides.subtitle: You don't need a big network. You need a real one.

slides.myth: Networking is awkward and only for extroverts.
slides.truth: Networking is just building relationships on purpose. You don't need to be outgoing — you need to be curious, reliable, and genuinely interested in others. Introverts often build deeper networks than extroverts because they go for quality over quantity.

slides.prompt: Think of one person you already know who works in a field you're curious about. What's one question you could ask them that would teach you something real about that career?

slides.title: Lesson 2.13 Takeaways
slides.subline: Skills prove what you can do. Relationships open doors.
takeaways: Networking = building real relationships, not collecting contacts
Communication, organization, digital skills, and professionalism matter everywhere
Start networking before you 'need' to — it takes time to build
Your network compounds: small consistent effort > burst of desperation

name: Internships and First Jobs
description: Your first job or internship is rarely about the paycheck. It's about building habits, earning references, and figuring out what you actually want to do with your time. This lesson covers how to get the most out of early work experiences.
objectives: Understand the real value of internships and first jobs beyond pay
Know what you should be trying to gain from early work experience
Start thinking about how to find and make the most of your first opportunity

slides.title: Internships and First Jobs
slides.subtitle: Unit 2 · Lesson 14
slides.detailText: Your first job or internship is rarely about the paycheck. It's about building habits, earning references, and figuring out what you actually want to do with your time. This lesson covers how to get the most out of early work experiences.

objectives: Understand the real value of internships and first jobs beyond pay
Know what you should be trying to gain from early work experience
Start thinking about how to find and make the most of your first opportunity

slides.question: What's the biggest value of an internship or first job?
options: The money you earn
The experience, habits, and connections you build
Nothing — they're a waste of time
explanations: Pay is real but usually not the main point at this stage. Entry-level pay is often low — the investment is in what you gain.
Exactly. Early jobs teach you how to work, who you are as an employee, and what you want more (or less) of in your career.
Not even close. Your first experience — even if it's not glamorous — shapes your habits, resume, and direction.

items.title: Work Habits
items.description: Punctuality, follow-through, and consistency — habits that follow you your entire career.

items.title: References
items.description: A manager who can vouch for your work is worth more than most resume lines in your early career.

items.title: Real Experience
items.description: You learn what a job actually looks like — not the version in a job description or a TV show.

items.title: Direction
items.description: You'll learn what you like, what you don't, and what you want to pursue next — all priceless information.

slides.quote: The goal of your first job isn't to find your passion. It's to learn how you work and start building a track record.

slides.title: How to Make the Most of a First Job
steps: Show up on time, every time — reliability is rare and noticed
Ask questions and stay curious — no one expects you to know everything
Do the unglamorous work well — small things prove your character
Build real relationships with coworkers and your manager
Ask for feedback — and actually act on it
slides.subtitle: You're not just earning money. You're building your reputation.

slides.prompt: What kind of first job or internship would you want — and what's one thing you'd want to gain from it beyond money? What's the first step to making it happen?

slides.title: Lesson 2.14 Takeaways
slides.subline: Your first job teaches you how to work — treat it seriously.
takeaways: The biggest value of early work is experience and habits, not pay
Reliability and curiosity will set you apart from day one
References from real managers are worth more than most credentials
Every early job teaches you what you want more — and less — of

name: Negotiating Pay and Growth
description: Most people never ask for more money — which means most people leave money on the table their entire careers. This lesson teaches you when to negotiate, how to prepare, and what to actually say.
objectives: Understand that negotiation is normal and expected — not rude
Know when the right time to negotiate is
Learn a simple, proven framework for asking for a raise or higher starting pay

slides.title: Negotiating Pay and Growth
slides.subtitle: Unit 2 · Lesson 15
slides.detailText: Most people never ask for more money — which means most people leave money on the table their entire careers. This lesson teaches you when to negotiate, how to prepare, and what to actually say.

objectives: Understand that negotiation is normal and expected — not rude
Know when the right time to negotiate is
Learn a simple, proven framework for asking for a raise or higher starting pay

slides.question: What's the best approach to negotiating your pay?
options: Randomly demand more money whenever you feel like it
Come prepared with results, timing, and a clear ask
Never negotiate — it makes you look ungrateful
explanations: Negotiating without preparation or a clear reason almost always backfires.
Exactly. Employers expect negotiation from confident candidates. Preparation is what makes the difference between a yes and a no.
This belief costs people thousands of dollars over their careers. Negotiation is professional and expected — not rude.

slides.definition:
A professional conversation about value — what you bring to the table and what you're asking in return. Negotiation isn't demanding or confrontational. It's presenting evidence of your worth and having a calm, prepared conversation about compensation.

Employers almost always expect candidates to negotiate. The first offer is rarely the final offer.

slides.myth: Asking for more money will make your employer angry or think less of you.
slides.truth: Most managers respect candidates who negotiate — it signals confidence and self-awareness. The real risk is not negotiating: studies consistently show that people who ask get more, and the downside of asking politely is almost always just 'no.'

slides.title: How to Ask for a Raise
steps: Know your market value — research what others in your role/area earn
Build your case — specific results, projects, or growth since your last pay review
Pick the right moment — after a win, before a review, not during a crunch
Ask clearly and confidently — state the number, don't hedge
Be prepared for any answer — know your response to yes, no, and 'not yet'
slides.subtitle: Preparation is what separates a raise from a rejection.

slides.scenario: You've worked at your part-time job for 8 months. You're reliable, always on time, and have taken on extra shifts. You want to ask for a raise.
slides.question: Which approach gives you the best shot?
options: Walk in and say 'I need more money'
Schedule time with your manager, come with specific examples of your reliability and contributions, and name the raise you're asking for
Wait and hope your manager notices on their own
explanations: Vague asks without proof rarely work — your manager has no reason to say yes.
Right. Timing + preparation + a specific ask is the formula. You've given your manager everything they need to say yes.
Hoping doesn't pay. Most raises don't happen unless you ask for them directly.

slides.prompt: Have you ever been afraid to ask for something you deserved — at work, school, or anywhere else? What held you back? What would you do differently with what you know now?

name: Budget Basics: The Concepts Behind the Numbers
description: Before you can build a budget, you need to understand the concepts that make it work — from spendable money to fixed payments, rollover, spending caps, and budget accuracy.
objectives: Know what your real spendable money actually is — it's not your full paycheck

slides.title: Budget Basics: The Concepts Behind the Numbers
slides.subtitle: Unit 3 · Lesson 3

slides.headerTitle: By the end of this lesson you will:
objectives: Know what your real spendable money actually is — it's not your full paycheck
Understand fixed payments and why they come first
Know what rollover money is and when to use it
Understand how to set spending limits and what happens when you hit them
Know how to spot whether your budget plan is actually working

slides.title: Your paycheck isn't your budget
slides.subtitle: There's an important number in between

slides.title: From Paycheck to Spendable Money
steps: You earn income — this is your starting number
Fixed payments come out first (bills, subscriptions, recurring costs you owe every month no matter what)
What's left after fixed payments is your real spendable money — sometimes called Available Bread in BreadHead
You then split THAT number across your budget categories
Whatever's left unspent at the end of the month can roll over or move to savings
slides.subtitle: Most people budget their full paycheck and wonder why they always run short. It's because the fixed payments already took their cut before you spent a single fun dollar.

slides.definition: Recurring costs that come out every month on a set schedule — whether you like it or not. Phone bill, rent, subscriptions, insurance, gym membership. These are non-negotiable and should always be accounted for before you allocate anything else.

slides.question: You earn $900 a month. Your phone bill is $60, gym is $30, and Spotify is $10. What is your actual spendable money?
options: $900 — that's what I earned
$800 — I subtracted the phone bill
$800 — I subtracted everything fixed
$810 — I only counted the big bills
explanations: $900 is your gross income before fixed costs. Never budget from this number.
You forgot the gym and Spotify — both are fixed monthly costs.
Correct! $60 + $30 + $10 = $100 in fixed payments. $900 − $100 = $800. That's your real starting point.
Subscriptions count. Every recurring charge matters no matter how small.

slides.definition: The total percentage of your income that is already locked into recurring bills before you spend anything. If your fixed payments add up to $200 on a $1,000 income, your fixed burden is 20%. A high fixed burden means less flexibility — and less room to save.

habits: Forgetting small subscriptions when planning your budget
Budgeting from your full paycheck instead of your spendable amount
Signing up for too many recurring charges until your fixed burden eats half your income
whyBadExplanations: Small subscriptions feel invisible but pile up fast — $8 here, $13 there, $5 somewhere else. By the time you notice, $50/month is just gone with nothing to show for it.
If you budget from your full paycheck, every fixed payment that hits feels like a surprise. You'll always end up short.

A creeping fixed burden is one of the most common ways people lose financial control. If more than 40–50% of your income is locked in recurring bills, you have a structural problem — not just a spending problem.

slides.definition: When you don't spend all the money in a budget category, you can "roll it over" — carry the unspent balance into next month's version of that category. For example, if your Fun budget is $100 and you only spent $60, you could start next month with $140 in Fun instead of resetting back to $100.

slides.title: Rollover: Use It or Reset?
slides.optionA: Roll over unspent Fun money to next month
slides.optionB: Reset every category to zero each month
slides.consequenceA: You had a quiet month — now next month you have a little extra room for a concert or a bigger night out. Intentional and rewarding.
slides.consequenceB: Clean slate every month. Simpler to manage, and stops you from building up a false sense of 'extra' money that quietly disappears.

slides.title: Soft Cap vs. Hard Cap
slides.leftBody: You get a warning when you hit your spending limit — but you can still keep spending. Good for awareness without restriction. The risk: it's easy to tap past the warning and keep going.
slides.rightBody: Spending is blocked once you hit your limit. You can't log more spend in that category until next month or until you adjust. More discipline, less flexibility — great for categories you know you overspend in.
slides.eyebrow: What happens when you go over budget?
slides.footer: Neither is wrong. Most people use soft caps on most categories and hard caps on one or two problem areas.

slides.definition: A measure of how close your spending plan was to what actually happened. If you planned to spend $150 on Food and spent $148, that's high accuracy. If you planned $150 and spent $310, that's low accuracy — and a signal that your plan needs to be adjusted, not your willpower.

slides.myth: If I go over budget, I failed.
slides.truth: Going over budget is information, not failure. It tells you which category was planned wrong — either your estimate was too low, or something unexpected happened. Good budgeters don't beat themselves up; they adjust the number and move on.

slides.prompt: What are your current fixed payments every month? List every recurring charge you can think of — phone, subscriptions, memberships, anything that hits automatically. Add them up. Does that number surprise you?

slides.title: Lesson 3.3 Takeaways
takeaways: Your spendable money = income minus fixed payments — always budget from this number
Fixed payments come first, every month, no exceptions
Rollover lets you carry unspent money forward — use it intentionally
Soft caps warn you; hard caps stop you — pick the right one per category
Budget accuracy tells you if your plan is realistic, not if you're a good person

slides.title: So Which Account Should You Use?
slides.optionA: Traditional Savings
slides.optionB: High-Yield Savings (HYSA)
slides.consequenceA: Easy in-person access, familiar big banks — but earns almost nothing (0.01%–0.5%). Fine if you need branch support, otherwise leaves money on the table.
slides.consequenceB: Online only, no branches — but earns 4%–5% interest with the exact same government protection. Almost always the better choice for emergency funds and short-term goals.

slides.title: When Each Account Actually Makes Sense
slides.leftBody: Emergency fund, short-term goals, any cash you might need in the next few years. The interest is free money and the risk is zero.
slides.rightBody: Long-term growth over decades. For that, investments like index funds inside a Roth IRA or 401(k) will grow far more — which is exactly what the next few lessons cover.

slides.definition: A CD is a savings account where you agree to leave your money untouched for a set period of time (e.g. 6 months, 1 year, 2 years) in exchange for a guaranteed interest rate — often slightly higher than a HYSA. The catch: if you withdraw early, you pay a penalty. Example: You lock $1,000 in a 1-year CD at 5.2% APY. At the end of the year you get your $1,000 + ~$52 guaranteed. But if you need that money in month 4, you lose some of the interest.

slides.title: HYSA vs. CD — Which Fits You?
slides.leftBody: Best for emergency funds and goals with no fixed timeline. Add or withdraw anytime. Rate can change month to month.
slides.rightBody: Best for money you know you won't need for a specific stretch of time. Rate is locked in — great if rates drop. But touching it early costs you.
slides.eyebrow: Both are safe. The difference is flexibility.
slides.footer: For most teens, a HYSA is the better starting point. CDs make more sense once you have a solid emergency fund already built.

slides.definition: Annual Percentage Yield is the real yearly return you earn on your savings, including the effect of compounding (interest earning interest). You can use it to compare banks. higher APY = more money in your pocket. Example: 5% APY on $1,000 = about $50 free after one year (with monthly compounding). Unlike simple "interest rate," APY shows the true growth.

name: Compound Interest
description: In this lesson you'll learn what compound interest is, how it turns small savings into big money over time, and why starting early gives you a huge advantage.
objectives: Compound interest = interest on interest
Starting early beats larger amounts started later
Consistency over time creates exponential growth

slides.definition: Interest calculated on your original money PLUS the interest you've already earned. It snowballs and growth gets faster over time. Example: $1,000 at 5% → Year 1: +$50 → Year 2: +$52.50 (5% on $1,050).

slides.title: Simple vs Compound
steps: Simple interest: interest only on original amount — forever
Compound interest: interest on growing balance — adds up way more
Banks compound monthly or daily in good accounts
Result: Exponential growth over decades

slides.title: Simple vs Compound — The Real Difference

contexts.text: Interest only on the original amount. $1,000 + $100/month at 5% for 10 years ≈ $15,900 total.
contexts.label: Simple Interest

contexts.text: Interest in growing balance, speeds up. Same $1,000 + $100/month at 5 % for 10 years ≈ $16,400 total

slides.definition: Compounding frequency means how often interest is added to your balance (daily, monthly, quarterly, or yearly). In general, the more often interest compounds, the more money you earn over time, because each new round of interest can start earning interest sooner.

name: HSA — The Triple Tax Win
description: Learn what a Health Savings Account is, why it's one of the most powerful savings tools available, and how it works for people with the right health plan.
objectives: HSA = triple tax advantage: pre-tax in, grows tax-free, tax-free out

slides.title: HSA — The Most Underrated Savings Account
slides.subtitle: Lesson 5.9

slides.definition: An HSA is a special savings account for medical expenses that comes with three tax advantages at once: you contribute pre-tax money, it grows tax-free, and you withdraw it tax-free when used for qualified medical costs. No other account does all three. Examples: Doctor visits, prescriptions, dental care, glasses and contacts, mental health services, and many other out-of-pocket health costs. The IRS has a full list, but everyday medical needs are almost always covered.

items.title: Contribute pre-tax
items.description: Money goes in before the government takes its cut — lowers your taxable income right now.

items.title: Grows tax-free
items.description: Any interest or investment growth inside the HSA is never taxed.

items.title: Withdraw tax-free
items.description: Spend on qualified medical costs (doctor visits, prescriptions, dental, vision) and pay zero tax on the way out.

items.title: Rolls over forever
items.description: Unlike some accounts, unused HSA money never expires. It just keeps growing year after year.

slides.myth: An HSA is just for paying doctor bills right now.
slides.truth: You can invest the money inside your HSA — just like a Roth IRA — and let it grow for decades. Many people use it as a stealth retirement account specifically for healthcare costs, which tend to be one of the biggest expenses in retirement.

slides.definition: You can only open an HSA if your health insurance is a High Deductible Health Plan — meaning it has a higher deductible (the amount you pay before insurance kicks in) than a standard plan. HDHPs usually have lower monthly premiums, common for younger, healthier people who don't visit the doctor often.

slides.question: What makes an HSA different from a regular savings account?
options: You can only use it at the pharmacy
It has a triple tax advantage — pre-tax in, tax-free growth, tax-free out for medical
It earns higher interest than a HYSA
explanations: It covers a wide range of qualified medical expenses — not just pharmacy.
Correct. No other savings account does all three.
Interest rates vary — the tax savings are the real power, not the rate.

habits: Using your HSA to pay every minor medical bill as soon as it arrives
whyBadExplanations: You can pay medical bills out of pocket now and reimburse yourself from the HSA years later — there's no deadline. The longer money stays invested inside the HSA, the more it compounds. Many savvy people pay small bills from their regular account, let the HSA grow untouched, and cash it all out in retirement. You can also use it for non-medical expenses after age 65, just like a traditional 401(k).

slides.definition: While saving is when you put money aside for short-term goals with low risk and easy access (like an emergency fund), investing uses money for long-term growth in things like stocks or bonds, giving higher potential returns but with greater risk and less immediate access

Investing is putting money into something today with the goal of generating income or appreciation (growth in value) over time. It's a process of putting your money to work for you, often in assets like stocks, bonds, or real estate, to help you achieve long-term financial goals.

slides.definition: Inflation is the gradual rise in prices over time — which means the same dollar buys a little less each year. Money sitting in a checking account earning 0% interest is slowly shrinking in real value. Investing is one of the main ways to stay ahead of inflation and make sure your money actually keeps its purchasing power. If inflation is 3% per year, $1,000 today buys only about $970 worth of stuff next year. Over 20 years at 3%, that $1,000 has the buying power of roughly $550. Investing at 7–10% yearly beats inflation and grows your wealth at the same time.

Some companies share a portion of their profits with shareholders on a regular schedule — usually quarterly. This cash payment is called a dividend. You don't have to sell any shares to receive it — it just lands in your account. ETFs and index funds can also pay dividends when the companies inside them do. You own 10 shares of a company that pays $0.50/share per quarter. Every 3 months you receive $5 automatically. Over years of reinvesting those dividends back into more shares, the compounding effect adds up significantly.

name: Stocks, Bonds, Index Funds, ETFs
description: In this lesson you will learn about stocks, bonds, index funds, ETFs, how they work, how they differ from each other, and why most smart investors use a mix of all of them.
objectives: Stocks = growth + ownership + possible dividends
Bonds = steady income + safety
Index funds and ETFs provide easy, cheap diversification
Rebalance once a year to keep your risk where you want it

slides.definition: Buying a tiny piece of a real company. If the company grows or profits, your share value usually rises, and vice versa. You can also get dividends (company profit share). Higher potential growth, higher ups & downs.

Lending money to a company or government for a set time. They pay you interest regularly and return principal at the end. Lower growth, much steadier. You get paid "rent" on your money for loaning it out.

When a company earns profit, it can reinvest it or pay some out to shareholders as dividends. Not all stocks pay them — growth companies (like tech startups) usually reinvest everything. Older, stable companies (think Coca-Cola, Johnson & Johnson) tend to pay reliable dividends. Many ETFs and index funds pass dividends through to you automatically. You hold a dividend ETF. Every quarter it deposits cash into your account from the dozens of companies inside it paying dividends. You set it to auto-reinvest — meaning those dividends buy more shares, which then earn more dividends. This is dividend compounding, and over decades it's a serious wealth builder.

items.title: Index Fund
items.description: Mutual fund that copies a market index (e.g., S&P 500). One purchase gives you a tiny share of all 500 biggest U.S. companies automatically.

items.title: ETF
items.description: Same as an index fund but trades like a stock all day. One buy = a tiny piece of all 500 companies. Lower fees, more flexible.

slides.definition: Over time, some investments grow faster than others — so your original mix drifts. If you planned 80% stocks and 20% bonds, after a big stock market year you might be sitting at 90/10 without doing anything. Rebalancing means selling a little of what grew and buying a little of what didn't to get back to your target. Most people do this once a year. You start the year at 80% stocks, 20% bonds. Stocks have a great year. By December you're at 88% stocks, 12% bonds. You sell some stock ETF and buy a little bond ETF to get back to 80/20. Simple, takes 10 minutes, and keeps your risk level where you want it.

name: Diversification
description: In this lesson you'll learn what diversification is, why it's one of the smartest moves in investing, and how to do it simply with ETFs and funds.

slides.definition: Not all investments move the same way. When some drop, others stay steady or rise. Diversification is owning a multitude of different stocks and bonds to smooth out the ride and protect your money long-term.

slides.myth: When the market drops, you should sell everything to protect yourself.
slides.truth: Market drops are normal — the S&P 500 has dropped 10% or more in a single year dozens of times, and it has recovered every time over the long run. Selling during a drop locks in the loss permanently. Staying put (or even buying more) is almost always the better move for a long-term investor. The people who panic sell are the ones who actually lose money. The people who hold or buy during drops are the ones who win.

slides.definition: As markets move, your investment mix drifts from your original plan. Rebalancing means adjusting back — selling a bit of what grew and buying a bit of what didn't — so your risk level stays where you intended. Do it once a year. It takes about 10 minutes and keeps your portfolio from accidentally becoming too risky or too conservative over time. You target 80% stocks, 20% bonds. After a great stock year you're at 90/10. You sell some stock ETF, buy some bond ETF, and you're back to 80/20.

slides.question: Diversification Guarantees You Won't Lose Money

slides.definition: A brokerage account is the account you open to buy and sell investments like stocks and ETFs. Think of it as a bank account, but instead of just holding cash, it holds your investments too. You deposit money into it and use it to buy whatever you want to invest in. The big ones — Fidelity, Schwab, Vanguard — are all free to open, charge no commissions on trades, and have no minimums. You open a Fidelity account, deposit $100, and buy $100 worth of VOO (S&P 500 ETF). That $100 is now invested and growing with the market. You can add money or check your balance anytime through the app.

If you're under 18, you can't open a brokerage account by yourself — but a parent or guardian can open a custodial account in your name. They are the legal owner until you turn 18 (or 21 in some states), at which point it transfers fully to you. It works exactly like a regular brokerage — you can buy ETFs, stocks, anything. Some platforms like Fidelity Youth also let teens 13+ manage their own account with parental oversight. Your parent opens a Fidelity custodial account for you. You both agree to invest $50/month into VTI. By the time you turn 18, you already have a growing portfolio and years of compounding behind you. On your 18th birthday, the account is fully yours.

Most brokerages let you buy a fraction of a share instead of a whole one. So if one share of Amazon costs $200 and you only have $20, you can buy 1/10th of a share. You still own a real piece of the company, you still receive your fraction of any dividends, and your investment grows proportionally. This completely removes the "I can't afford to invest" excuse. VOO (S&P 500 ETF) costs around $500 per share. With $10 you own 0.02 shares. Your $10 grows exactly as if you owned the full share — just proportionally. $10 invested now at 8% average for 40 years = roughly $217. Starting with $10 is infinitely better than starting with nothing.

name: Capital Gains: When the IRS Gets a Cut

slides.title: Capital Gains — When the IRS Gets a Cut
slides.subtitle: Lesson 6.7

slides.definition: A capital gain is the profit you make when you sell an investment for more than you paid for it. The IRS counts this as income — meaning you owe tax on it. You only owe the tax when you actually sell. If your investment is up 50% but you haven't sold, you owe nothing yet. The moment you sell and lock in the profit, the tax clock starts. You buy $500 of an ETF. It grows to $700. You sell. Your capital gain is $200 — and you'll owe tax on that $200, not the full $700.

slides.title: The most important rule in investing tax
slides.leftBody: Sold an investment you held for less than 1 year. Taxed at your regular income tax rate — the same rate as your paycheck. Can be 10%, 22%, or higher depending on your income.
slides.rightBody: Sold an investment you held for more than 1 year. Taxed at a much lower rate — 0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income. Most teens and young adults pay 0% on long-term gains.
slides.eyebrow: Hold for at least one year — it makes a huge difference
slides.footer: Holding for just one extra day past the 1-year mark can save you a significant amount in taxes. It's one of the simplest and most powerful tax moves in investing.

slides.question: You bought an ETF 8 months ago and it's up $300. You sell today. How is that gain taxed?
options: At the lower long-term rate — you've held it long enough
At your regular income tax rate — it's a short-term gain
You don't owe any tax on investment gains
explanations: You need to hold for more than 1 full year to qualify for the lower long-term rate. 8 months doesn't cut it.
Correct. Under 1 year = short-term = taxed like regular income.
Capital gains are taxable income. Always.

habits: Selling a great long-term investment early just to lock in profits, triggering a higher short-term tax rate
Never selling anything ever because you're scared of taxes, even when it makes financial sense to rebalance
whyBadExplanations: Taxes are a cost of investing, not a punishment. The goal is to pay less of them by holding long-term when possible — but not to let fear of taxes stop you from making smart moves. A $300 gain you pay 15% tax on is still $255 in your pocket. That beats holding forever and never using your money.

slides.title: Health Insurance: How It Actually Works
slides.subtitle: Lesson 7.4

slides.definition: A copay is a fixed amount you pay for a covered health care service, regardless of what the visit costs. It's due at the time of the appointment. Example: Your plan has a $20 copay for primary care visits and a $50 copay for specialist visits. You see your doctor for a cold — you pay $20 at the desk, insurance handles the rest.

After you've met your deductible, coinsurance is the percentage of costs you still pay while your insurance covers the rest. A common split is 80/20 — insurance pays 80%, you pay 20%. Example: You've met your deductible. You get a procedure that costs $500. With 80/20 coinsurance, you pay $100 and insurance pays $400.

The out-of-pocket maximum is the most you will ever have to pay in a single year for covered services. Once you hit it, insurance pays 100% of covered costs for the rest of the year — no copays, no coinsurance, nothing. Example: Your out-of-pocket max is $4,000. You have a bad year with a surgery and several follow-ups. Once your total payments hit $4,000, every remaining covered visit that year is completely free to you.

slides.title: In-Network vs Out-of-Network
slides.leftBody: Doctors and hospitals that have an agreement with your insurance company. Your plan covers a larger share of costs. Copays and coinsurance apply as normal. Always try to stay in-network.
slides.rightBody: Providers with no agreement with your insurer. You pay a much larger share — sometimes everything. Some plans don't cover out-of-network at all except in emergencies.
slides.eyebrow: One of the most expensive mistakes people make
slides.footer: Always check whether a doctor is in-network before booking. One out-of-network visit can cost hundreds more than expected.

slides.definition: Open enrollment is the specific period each year when you can sign up for, change, or drop a health insurance plan. Outside this window, you generally cannot make changes unless you have a qualifying life event. For ACA marketplace plans it typically runs November 1 to January 15. Employer plans have their own windows, usually in the fall. Example: Your employer's open enrollment runs October 15–31. If you miss it and don't have a qualifying event, you're locked into your current plan (or no plan) for the next full year.

Certain life events trigger a Special Enrollment Period — a 60-day window to sign up for or change coverage outside of open enrollment. These events include losing coverage, turning 26, getting married, having a baby, or moving to a new state. Example: You turn 26 in April and age off your parent's plan. You now have 60 days to enroll in a new plan through your employer or the marketplace — even though open enrollment is months away.

slides.definition: A grace period is a set number of days after a missed premium payment during which your coverage remains active. Two years later it's worth $18,000 but you still owe $21,000. Your car gets totaled. Regular insurance pays $18,000. Without gap insurance, you owe the lender $3,000 out of pocket for a car you can no longer drive. With gap insurance, that $3,000 is covered.

name: How Jobs Are Taxed
description: In this lesson you will learn how taxes show up when you earn money from a job, why your paycheck is usually smaller than your total earnings, and how to actually read a pay stub.
objectives: The amount you earn is not always the amount you take home.
Taxes can be taken out of your pay before you get it.

slides.definition: Gross pay is the total amount of money you earned before taxes or other deductions are taken out.
Net pay is the amount of money you actually take home after taxes and other deductions are taken out.

slides.title: What Can Happen to Your Paycheck

items.title: Gross Pay
items.description: This is the full amount you earned before anything is taken out.

items.title: Taxes Withheld
items.description: Some money may be taken out for taxes before you get paid.

items.title: Payroll Taxes
items.description: Part of your paycheck may go to Social Security and Medicare.

items.title: Net Pay
items.description: This is the amount that actually lands in your bank account or on your paycheck.

slides.definition: A pay stub is a document that comes with your paycheck. It shows how much you earned, what was taken out, and what you actually received. It is your proof of income and your record of withholding.

slides.title: The Main Sections of a Pay Stub
steps: Gross Pay — The total you earned before anything is removed.
Federal Income Tax Withheld — The amount sent toward federal taxes.
State Income Tax Withheld — Applies in most states; may be zero if you live in a no-income-tax state.
Social Security (OASDI) — 6.2% of your gross pay, up to the annual limit.
Medicare — 1.45% of your gross pay.
Other Deductions — Could include health insurance, retirement contributions, or other benefits.
Net Pay — What's left after all deductions. This is what hits your account.

slides.title: What Does YTD Mean on a Pay Stub?
slides.prompt: You see 'YTD' next to every number on your pay stub. What is it?
slides.revealedContent: YTD stands for Year-to-Date. It shows the running total of that line item since January 1 of the current year. So 'Federal Tax YTD: $340' means $340 total has been withheld for federal taxes so far this year across all your paychecks — not just this one.

slides.question: You earned $400 this week. Your pay stub shows Federal Tax: $28, Social Security: $24.80, Medicare: $5.80. What is your approximate net pay?
options: About $400
About $341
About $200
About $450
explanations: ❌ Nope. That would be your gross pay before deductions.
✅ That's right! $400 minus $28 minus $24.80 minus $5.80 = $341.40. That's your net pay.
❌ Not quite. The deductions reduce your check, but not by that much at this income level.
❌ Nope. Net pay is always less than or equal to gross pay — money is taken out, not added.

slides.title: How a Paycheck Gets Smaller
steps: First, you work and earn money.
Your total earnings show up as gross pay.
Taxes and other deductions may be taken out.
What is left becomes your net pay.
Your net pay is the amount you actually receive.

habits: Spending based on gross pay instead of net pay — and throwing away pay stubs without looking at them.

Your hours did not count because you are a student.
