✅ That's right! Your gross pay may be $160, but your net pay can be lower after taxes.
❌ Not quite. Being a student does not cancel out your work hours.
❌ Nope. The most likely reason is taxes or deductions, not a random pay cut.

slides.title: How Jobs Are Taxed Recap
takeaways: Gross pay is what you earn before anything is taken out.
Net pay is what you actually take home.
A pay stub shows every deduction between gross and net.
YTD figures show your running totals for the year.
Save your pay stubs and always plan around net pay, not gross.

name: Withholdings and Payroll Taxes
description: In this lesson you will learn what withholdings and payroll taxes are, why money gets taken out of a paycheck automatically, where that money goes, and how the W-4 form controls how much is withheld in the first place.
objectives: Not all money taken from your paycheck is the same kind of tax.
Withholding is money taken out ahead of time for taxes.
Payroll taxes help fund Social Security and Medicare.
The W-4 is the form you fill out at the start of a job that tells your employer how much to withhold.

slides.definition: Withholding is money taken out of your paycheck before you receive it. It is sent toward your taxes ahead of time instead of making you pay it all later.

A W-4 is a form you fill out when you start a new job. It tells your employer how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck. It is not a tax return — it just sets up your withholding before any money moves.

slides.title: W-4 vs. W-2 — Easy to Mix Up, Very Different

items.title: W-4 (You Fill Out)
items.description: You fill this out on day one of the job. It tells your employer what to withhold.

items.title: W-2 (Employer Sends You)
items.description: Your employer sends this after the year ends. It shows what you actually earned and what was withheld.

items.title: When: W-4
items.description: Before your first paycheck.

items.title: When: W-2
items.description: After the year ends, usually by January 31.

slides.title: What Gets Taken Out of a Paycheck?

items.title: Federal Income Tax
items.description: This is money withheld for federal income taxes.

items.title: State Income Tax
items.description: In some states, money is also withheld for state income taxes.

items.title: Social Security
items.description: This payroll tax helps fund benefits for older adults and some disabled workers.

items.title: Medicare
items.description: This payroll tax helps fund part of the U.S. health insurance system for older adults.

slides.question: What does "withholding" mean on a paycheck?
options: Your employer is keeping part of your pay for no reason
Money is being taken out ahead of time for taxes
Your bank charges you every payday
You lose money forever and can never get it back
explanations: ❌ Nope. That is not what withholding means.
✅ That's right! Withholding means part of your pay is being sent toward taxes before you get the check.
❌ Not quite. Bank fees are a different thing.
❌ Nope. Withholding goes toward taxes, and in some cases too much withholding can lead to a refund later.

slides.question: What is the purpose of filling out a W-4?
options: To apply for a job
To tell your employer how much tax to withhold from your paycheck
To file your taxes with the government
To prove you are allowed to work
explanations: ❌ Nope. A W-4 comes after you already have the job.
✅ That's right! The W-4 sets up withholding before your first check.
❌ Not quite. Filing taxes happens separately, usually in the spring.
❌ Nope. That is what an I-9 form is for — a different form entirely.

slides.definition: Payroll taxes are taxes taken from a paycheck to help fund programs like Social Security and Medicare. These are separate from federal income tax.

slides.title: Same Thing or Different Things?
slides.optionA: Federal income tax withholding
slides.optionB: Payroll taxes
slides.consequenceA: This is money sent ahead toward income taxes you may owe.
slides.consequenceB: These are separate paycheck taxes that help fund Social Security and Medicare.

slides.title: How to Handle a W-4 as a Teen
steps: Get the W-4 from your employer on your first day.
Read the instructions — for most teens with one job and no dependents, it is simple.
Enter your name, address, Social Security number, and filing status.
If you are a dependent and earned below a certain amount, you may be able to claim exempt — check the instructions carefully.
Sign and date the form and return it to your employer.
If your situation changes (second job, big life change), you can update your W-4 at any time.

slides.title: What Happens If You Claim 'Exempt' on a W-4?
slides.prompt: Some teens can write 'Exempt' on their W-4. What does that mean?
slides.revealedContent: Claiming exempt means no federal income tax is withheld from your paycheck. You can only do this if you had no tax liability last year and expect none this year. If you claim exempt but actually owe taxes, you'll owe them all at once when you file — plus possible penalties.

slides.scenario: You look at your paycheck and see money taken out for federal tax, Social Security, and Medicare. What likely happened?
slides.question: What likely happened?
options: Your employer probably made a mistake.
Some of the money was withheld for income taxes, and some was taken for payroll taxes.
The government only taxes adults, so this should not happen.
explanations: ❌ Nope. Those are all normal paycheck deductions for many workers.
✅ That's right! Different taxes can come out of the same paycheck for different reasons.
❌ Not quite. If you have a job, taxes can absolutely show up on your paycheck.

slides.title: How Withholding Works
steps: You earn money from your job.
Your employer calculates what needs to be taken out based on your W-4.
Some money may be withheld for income taxes.
Some money may also be taken for Social Security and Medicare.
The rest becomes your take-home pay.
Later, your tax forms help show what was already paid.

habits: Ignoring the W-4 or thinking every dollar taken out of a paycheck is the same thing.
whyBadExplanations: Your W-4 directly controls how much comes out of every paycheck. And withholding, payroll taxes, and income tax are all different things — confusing them makes paychecks and tax forms much harder to understand.

contexts.text: Waiting until later to pay all your taxes at once
contexts.label: Bigger surprise later

contexts.text: Having some money taken out little by little from each paycheck
contexts.label: Smaller pieces along the way

slides.title: Withholdings and Payroll Taxes Recap
takeaways: Withholding means money is taken out ahead of time for taxes.
The W-4 is the form you fill out at the start of a job — it sets up your withholding.
Payroll taxes are different from income tax.
Social Security and Medicare are common payroll taxes.
A paycheck can include several different tax deductions at once.

name: W-2s, 1099s, and Self-Employment Tax
description: In this lesson you will learn the difference between W-2 and 1099 income, why that difference matters for taxes, and what happens to taxes when you work for yourself or do freelance work.
objectives: W-2 workers are employees, and taxes are often taken out automatically.
1099 workers are usually independent contractors, and taxes are usually not taken out automatically.
Self-employed workers pay both the employee and employer share of FICA — 15.3% — before income tax.
The form you get affects how you plan, save, and track your money.

slides.definition: A W-2 is a tax form usually given to employees. It shows how much money you earned from a job and how much was already taken out for taxes.
A 1099 is a tax form often used for independent contractors or freelancers. It usually shows how much you were paid, but taxes often were not taken out along the way.

Self-employment tax is the combined Social Security and Medicare tax that self-employed people pay entirely on their own. At a regular job, you pay 7.65% and your employer pays 7.65%. When you work for yourself, you pay both halves — 15.3% total — before income tax is even calculated.

items.title: W-2 Employee
items.description: You work for an employer, and taxes are usually withheld from your paycheck.

items.title: 1099 Contractor
items.description: You work more independently, and you are usually responsible for setting aside money for taxes yourself.

items.title: Take-Home Pay
items.description: A 1099 payment may look bigger at first because less or nothing was taken out yet.

items.title: Record Keeping
items.description: With 1099 income, it becomes even more important to track what you earn and save for taxes.

contexts.text: W-2 Employee: You pay 7.65% FICA. Your employer pays 7.65% FICA on your behalf. Income tax is withheld each check.
contexts.label: Split with your employer

contexts.text: 1099 Contractor: You pay 15.3% FICA yourself. No withholding. You handle income tax separately.
contexts.label: You cover the whole thing

slides.question: What is the biggest difference between W-2 and 1099 income?
options: W-2 income is always higher than 1099 income
1099 income means you never have to pay taxes
W-2 jobs usually withhold taxes, while 1099 jobs usually do not
Only adults can receive 1099 income
explanations: ❌ Nope. Either one can pay more depending on the job.
❌ Definitely not. You may actually need to plan more carefully for taxes with 1099 income.
✅ That's right! That is one of the biggest practical differences.
❌ Nope. Teens can receive 1099 income too, depending on the work they do.

slides.question: You earn $1,000 freelancing. Before income tax, approximately how much self-employment tax do you owe?
options: About $76
About $153
Nothing — contractors don't pay FICA
About $300
explanations: ❌ Not quite. That would be just your half of FICA as a W-2 employee — but as a freelancer you pay both halves.
✅ That's right! 15.3% × $1,000 = $153 in self-employment tax alone, before any income tax.
❌ Definitely not. Contractors pay more FICA than employees, not less.
❌ Not quite. $300 would be closer to adding income tax on top — 15.3% is just the self-employment tax portion.

slides.title: Bigger Check Now or Fewer Surprises Later?
slides.optionA: Get paid as a 1099 contractor with no taxes taken out
slides.optionB: Get paid as a W-2 employee with taxes withheld
slides.consequenceA: The payment may look bigger now, but you may owe a lot more later if you do not set money aside.
slides.consequenceB: The check may look smaller, but taxes are already being handled along the way.

slides.scenario: Two students each earn $500. One earns it from a part-time W-2 job at a store. The other earns it freelancing and gets paid as a contractor. What does this mean?
slides.question: What does this mean?
options: The student with the 1099 automatically got the better deal because the payment looks bigger.
The student with the W-2 may take home less now, but the student with the 1099 may need to set money aside for taxes.
There is no real difference as long as both made $500.
explanations: ❌ Nope. A bigger payment now does not always mean a better deal after taxes.
✅ That's right! The difference is not just how much they earned, but how the taxes are handled.
❌ Not quite. The tax setup can make those two situations feel very different later.

slides.definition: Estimated taxes are payments you make to the IRS four times a year if you have income that doesn't have taxes automatically withheld. Self-employed workers and 1099 contractors often need to make these payments to avoid a large bill and penalties in April.

slides.title: How to Handle W-2 vs. 1099 Income
steps: Ask whether you are being treated as an employee or an independent worker.
Check whether taxes are being taken out of your pay.
If you are getting 1099 income, track every dollar you earn.
Set aside approximately 25–30% of each 1099 payment for taxes — this covers self-employment tax and income tax for most teens.
Keep that money in a separate savings account so you do not accidentally spend it.
If your side hustle income is significant, look into making quarterly estimated tax payments.
Keep tax forms and payment records in one place, and track any business expenses too — they can reduce what you owe.

slides.scenario: You made $3,000 designing logos for clients this year. No one withheld any taxes. At tax time, what do you likely owe before any deductions?
slides.question: What do you likely owe before any deductions?
options: Nothing — it was just side work, not a real job.
Around $459 in self-employment tax alone, plus income tax on top.
The same as a W-2 worker who earned $3,000.
Just whatever was listed on the 1099 form.
explanations: ❌ Nope. The IRS treats freelance income as real income regardless of how you think of it.
✅ That's right. 15.3% × $3,000 = $459 in SE tax, and you may owe income tax on top of that too.
❌ Not quite. A W-2 worker's employer paid half of FICA for them. You pay all of it as a freelancer.
❌ Nope. The 1099 shows what you were paid — it doesn't calculate your tax. That's your job.

habits: Spending all your 1099 money because it feels like extra cash.
whyBadExplanations: As a freelancer you owe 15.3% in self-employment tax before income tax is even added. Spending it all and then owing a large bill you can't pay is one of the most common mistakes young freelancers make.

slides.title: W-2s, 1099s, and Self-Employment Tax Recap
takeaways: W-2 income usually comes from employee jobs with taxes withheld.
1099 income usually comes from contract or freelance work with no automatic withholding.
Self-employed workers pay 15.3% in self-employment tax before income tax.
Set aside 25–30% of every freelance payment for taxes.
The form you get affects how you plan, save, and track your money.

name: Deductions, Tax Brackets, and Refunds
description: In this lesson you will learn what deductions, tax brackets, and tax refunds are, what the standard deduction is and why most teens use it, and why a refund does not mean the government gave you extra money.
objectives: Deductions can lower the amount of income that gets taxed.
Most teens use the standard deduction, which is a fixed amount.
Tax brackets do not mean all your money is taxed at one rate.
A tax refund usually means too much was taken out earlier.

slides.definition: A deduction is something that lowers the amount of income that gets taxed. This can reduce how much tax you owe.
A tax bracket is a range of income that gets taxed at a certain rate. Not all of your income is taxed at the same rate.

The standard deduction is a fixed dollar amount the IRS lets you subtract from your income before calculating tax. Most people, including most teens, use the standard deduction instead of listing individual expenses. For 2024, the standard deduction for a single filer is $14,600.

slides.title: Standard vs. Itemized — What's the Difference?
slides.prompt: What does 'itemizing' mean, and why do most teens not do it?
slides.revealedContent: Itemizing means listing every individual deduction (mortgage interest, charity donations, etc.) and adding them up. Most teens don't have enough of these to beat the standard deduction amount, so the standard deduction is simpler and usually better.

slides.title: Three Tax Ideas People Mix Up

items.title: Deductions
items.description: Deductions can reduce the amount of income that gets taxed.

items.title: Tax Brackets
items.description: Different parts of income can be taxed at different rates.

items.title: Refunds
items.description: A refund usually means too much money was withheld earlier and is being returned.

slides.question: What does it usually mean if you get a tax refund?
options: The government decided to give you free bonus money
You probably had too much money withheld during the year
You paid no taxes at all
Your employer made a mistake every time
explanations: ❌ Nope. A refund is usually not free extra money.
✅ That's right! A refund usually means you paid in more than you ended up owing.
❌ Not quite. A refund usually means taxes were already taken out.
❌ Nope. A refund does not automatically mean something went wrong.

slides.title: Free Money or Your Money Coming Back?
slides.optionA: "A refund is free cash from the government."
slides.optionB: "A refund means too much was taken out earlier."
slides.consequenceA: This is not true. That idea confuses a lot of people.
slides.consequenceB: That's the idea. A tax refund is your own money coming back.

slides.scenario: Your friend says, "I do not want a raise because I'll move into a higher tax bracket and lose money." What should you make of this?
slides.question: What should you make of this?
options: They are right. Earning more can make your whole income get taxed so heavily that you lose money overall.
They are wrong. Moving into a higher bracket does not mean all of your income gets taxed at that higher rate.
They are right because raises are always bad for taxes.
explanations: ❌ Nope. That is a very common misunderstanding.
✅ That's right! Only the portion of income above the bracket line gets taxed at the higher rate.
❌ Not quite. Earning more money still means you are earning more money.

slides.title: A way to think about refunds
steps: You earn money during the year.
Some tax money gets withheld from your paychecks.
Later, your tax return compares what was withheld to what you actually owed.
If too much was withheld, you may get a refund.
If too little was withheld, you may owe money.
Either way, the refund is not random free money.

habits: Treating a tax refund like surprise bonus money.
whyBadExplanations: A refund usually means you got your own money back, so it still needs to be handled thoughtfully.

slides.title: Deductions, Tax Brackets, and Refunds Recap
takeaways: Deductions can lower taxable income.
The standard deduction is a fixed amount most teens use — $14,600 for a single filer in 2024.
Tax brackets do not mean all income is taxed the same way.
Earning more does not automatically hurt you.
A refund usually means too much was withheld earlier.

name: Filing Basics for Teens
description: In this lesson you will learn what filing taxes means, what forms teens may need, how to handle the basic steps without panicking, and where to find free tools to help you file.
objectives: Filing taxes means reporting income and tax information to the government.
The forms you receive help you fill out your tax return.
Teens may need to file taxes if they earned income during the year.
Most teens qualify for completely free filing through IRS Free File or VITA.

slides.title: Basic Tax Forms Teens may See

items.title: W-2
items.description: This form shows how much you earned as an employee and how much tax was already taken out.
This form shows money paid for freelance, contract, or other non-employee work.

items.title: Pay Records
items.description: Pay stubs can help you double-check your income and what was taken out during the year.

items.title: Tax Return
items.description: A tax return is the set of forms you file to report income and calculate whether you owe money or get a refund.

slides.question: What does it mean to file taxes?
options: To send your income and tax information to the government
To ask your employer for more money
To open a bank account
To pay every dollar you earned to the government
explanations: ✅ That's right! Filing means reporting what you earned and other tax details using forms.
❌ Nope. That has nothing to do with filing taxes.
❌ Not quite. Filing taxes and banking are different things.
❌ Nope. Filing is reporting information, not giving up all your money.

items.title: IRS Free File
items.description: If your income is below $79,000 (as of 2024), you can file your federal taxes for free at IRS.gov/freefile.

items.title: VITA
items.description: Volunteer Income Tax Assistance offers free in-person tax help from IRS-certified volunteers for people earning $67,000 or less.

items.title: IRS Free Fillable Forms
items.description: The IRS also offers free electronic fillable forms for any income level if you are comfortable doing the math yourself.

items.title: State Free File
items.description: Most states also offer free filing options. Check your state's Department of Revenue website.

slides.title: Toss the Forms or Keep Them?
slides.optionA: Lose your forms and try to remember everything later
slides.optionB: Keep your tax forms and use them to help with taxes
slides.consequenceA: This is a bad idea. Missing forms makes filing much more difficult and stressful
slides.consequenceB: This is miles better. Being organized is the first step to success in anything.

slides.scenario: You had a part-time job during the year and your employer sends you a W-2 form. What should you do with it?
slides.question: What should you do with it?
options: Ignore it because you can do taxes by yourself
Throw it away after you read it
Keep the form and use it when it is time to file.
explanations: ❌ Nope. Doing taxes by memory is a recipe for disaster
❌ Not exactly. Keeping track of important tax forms is important, and will make your life much easier.
✅ That's right! A W-2 is one of the main forms used when filing taxes

slides.title: Basic Filing Steps for Teens
steps: Collect your forms, such as W-2s or 1099s.
Keep your pay records and personal information together.
Check whether you qualify for IRS Free File or a local VITA site — most teens do.
Use the information from your forms to fill out your tax return.
Check your numbers before submitting anything.
File by the deadline.
Save copies of what you filed.

slides.question: A teen who earned $8,000 at a part-time job wants to file taxes. Which option makes the most sense?
options: Pay $100 to a tax preparer because taxes are complicated.
Use IRS Free File or VITA since their income is well within the free filing range.
Skip filing since teens don't owe much anyway.
Only file if their employer tells them to.
explanations: ❌ Not for a simple return like this. That is completely unnecessary.
✅ That's right! A simple return at this income level can be filed for free.
❌ Nope. If taxes were withheld, filing is how you get a refund. Skipping means leaving money behind.
❌ Not quite. Whether or not to file is based on your income and situation, not your employer's instructions.

habits: Ignoring tax forms because you think they don't matter — or paying to file when you don't have to.
whyBadExplanations: If you earn money, tax forms matter, and losing them creates problems. And most teens qualify for completely free filing — there is no reason to pay a service to do a simple return.

slides.definition: A tax return is the form or set of forms used to report income, taxes paid, and whether you owe more or get money back.

slides.title: Don't Pay to File for Free
slides.message: Most teens earning from part-time or gig work qualify for completely free federal filing. Before you pay anyone to do your taxes, check IRS.gov/freefile and search for a VITA site near you. Filing for free is not a trick — it is a program the government runs specifically so people do not have to pay to comply with the law.

slides.title: Filing Basics for Teens Recap
takeaways: Filing taxes means reporting income and tax information.
W-2s and 1099s are important forms to keep.
Being a teen does not mean tax forms do not matter.
Most teens qualify for free filing through IRS Free File or VITA.
Staying organized makes filing much easier.
Filing late or incorrectly can lead to penalties, delays, and more trouble.

name: Important Things to Remember with Taxes
description: In this lesson you will learn about deadlines, filing requirements, different tax treatments, and common myths that trip up teen filers.
objectives: Tax deadlines matter — April 15 every year.
Not all money is taxed the same way.
Teen income from jobs or side hustles can create different tax responsibilities.
Federal and state taxes are separate — always check your state's rules.

slides.title: Important Things to Remember with Taxes
slides.subtitle: Lesson 8.8

slides.definition: Filing late means missing the tax deadline. Filing incorrectly means submitting wrong information, missing income, or making mistakes on the return. Both can cause problems.

slides.title: Problems Caused by Late or Incorrect Filing

items.title: Penalties
items.description: Filing late can lead to penalties, which means extra money owed.

items.title: Delays
items.description: Mistakes on a return can slow everything down, including refunds.

items.title: Corrections
items.description: Incorrect filing can mean you have to fix forms, resend information, or respond to notices.

items.title: Fees
items.description: Filing late means a 5% penalty on unfiled taxes per month, up to 25%, as well as interest if you owe money.

slides.scenario: You were supposed to file taxes, but you waited too long and then rushed through the forms with mistakes. What might happen?
slides.question: What might happen?
options: Nothing happens as long as you did your best.
You can face delays, penalties, and have to correct the return later
The government will fix mistakes for you
explanations: ❌ Unfortunately, trying hard won't cut it. Any mistakes will cause problems.
✅ That's right! Both late filing and incorrect filing can create extra work and extra cost
❌ Not true. Some mistakes might get flagged, but you still have to do the work.

slides.definition: A tax deadline is the date by which you are supposed to file your taxes. The hard deadline is April 15 every year.

slides.question: Why does the tax deadline matter?
options: It's a recommendation, so you can file afterwards too
It is the day that you get a raise at your job
It only matters if you made more than $50,000 this year
It tells you when you are supposed to file your tax return
explanations: ❌ Nope. The deadline is hard, and missing it can cause big problems for you.
❌ Nope. That has nothing to do with tax day.
❌ Not true. If you made the minimum amount required to file, you need to file.
✅ That's right! Filing by the deadline helps you avoid penalties and delays.

slides.definition: There is not a single minimum amount of money to file taxes for everyone, and it can vary based on age, filing status, and whether someone can claim you as a dependent. It's recommended that you do some research to see the rules your state has in place for your situation.
Taxable money is money that counts for tax purposes. Non-taxable money is money that does not get taxed in the same way. Different kinds of money can be treated differently

slides.myth: I made under $20,000 so I definitely don't need to file.
slides.truth: Filing thresholds are lower than most people think, depend on your dependent status, and change each year. If you had taxes withheld, filing is how you get a refund. When in doubt, file.

slides.myth: Cash jobs are invisible to the IRS.
slides.truth: Cash income is still legally taxable income. It's your responsibility to report it whether or not you receive a form.

slides.myth: My parents claim me as a dependent so I don't have to file anything.
slides.truth: Being a dependent doesn't automatically mean you don't have to file. If you earned above the threshold for dependents, you still may need to file your own return.

items.title: Federal Tax
items.description: Federal income tax goes to the U.S. government and applies to everyone in the country who meets the filing threshold.

items.title: State Tax
items.description: State income tax is set by each state. Most states have it, but nine states (including Texas, Florida, and Washington) have no state income tax.

items.title: They're Separate
items.description: You may file a federal return and a state return separately. They have different forms, different deadlines (sometimes), and different rules.

items.title: Check Your State
items.description: Always look up your specific state's rules, because they vary a lot.

slides.title: Common Examples of Money and Taxes

items.title: Job Income
items.description: Money from a regular job is taxable income.

items.title: Tips or Side Work
items.description: Tips, freelance work, and gig income can also be taxable.

items.title: Gifts
items.description: Gift money is not treated the same way as money you earn from work.

items.title: Scholarships
items.description: Scholarship money can be treated differently depending on how it is used.

slides.scenario: You got money from three places this year: a part-time job, birthday money from grandma, and some paid design work you did for a neighbor. Which incomes are important here?
slides.question: Which incomes are important here?
options: None of it because taxes are a societal construct that you need to break free from
All of it is taxed the exact same way.
Money from jobs or paid work can create tax responsibilities, but gift money is different
explanations: ❌ If that's your thing then go for it :/
❌ Not quite. Different kinds of money can be treated differently.
✅ Right on the money. Earned money and gift money are not treated the same way.

items.title: Part-Time Job
items.description: If you work for a store, restaurant, or other employer, you may get a W-2.

items.title: Freelance or Gig Work
items.description: If you do design, editing, tutoring, or online work, you may need to track that income yourself.

items.title: Cash Jobs
items.description: Even if you are paid in cash, that money does not become invisible.

items.title: Reselling
items.description: Buying and reselling things for money can create income you may need to track.

slides.title: Things to Keep in Mind About Taxes Recap
takeaways: Tax deadlines matter — April 15 every year.
Not all money is taxed the same way.
Teen income from jobs or side hustles can create different tax responsibilities.
There is not one universal minimum income for filing taxes.
Federal and state taxes are separate — always check your state's rules.
Federal filing depends on your situation, and state filing rules differ from state to state.

name: Financial Scams and Fraud
description: Learn how common scams work, how to spot warning signs, and what to do if you think you were targeted.
objectives: Scams often use urgency, fear, or excitement
If someone wants your money or personal information fast, slow down
Anyone can get scammed
Acting quickly after a scam can reduce the damage

slides.definition: A scam is a dishonest trick used to steal money, personal information, or account access. While you've likely heard about scams before, it's best to 100% understand what they are.

items.title: Phishing
items.description: Fake emails, texts, or messages that try to get your password, bank info, or login code.

items.title: Fake Scholarships
items.description: These promise scholarship money but ask for a fee or personal information first.

items.title: Investment Scams
items.description: These offer fast, easy, or "guaranteed" profits with little or no risk.

items.title: Identity Theft
items.description: This happens when someone uses your personal information to open accounts, spend money, or pretend to be you.

slides.question: What is the biggest warning sign that something might be a scam?
options: A company logo appears in the message
The message pressures you to act immediately
The message sounds polite and professional
A friend sent you the link
explanations: While some scammers can copy logos and make messages look official, that's not the biggest indicator.
Urgency is one of the biggest red flags because it makes people react before thinking.
Some scams might seem like it, but this is not the biggest indicator.
Your friend isn't trying to steal your money! (hopefully)

slides.title: Real company or scam pressure?
slides.optionA: "Take some time to review this and contact us through our official website."
slides.optionB: "Send your info in the next 10 minutes or your account will be closed."
slides.consequenceA: This is much safer. Real businesses usually give you time to check, and won't ask for your credit card out of the blue.
slides.consequenceB: That's a huge red flag. Scammers use panic and urgency to get you.

slides.scenario: You get a text saying your bank account is locked. It includes a link and tells you to log in right away.
slides.question: What should you do?
options: Click the link and log in right away.
Open your bank's official app or website, or call the number on your card.
Reply to the text and ask if it is real.
explanations: This is risky because the link could go to a fake site that steals your login information.
This is the best choice because you are checking through an official source instead of trusting the text.
Replying can confirm that your number is active and may lead to more scam messages.

slides.title: What to do if you think it's a scam
steps: Stop and do not click, send money, or share personal information.
Check the claim using an official website, app, or phone number you found yourself.
Take screenshots or save the message.
Change your password if you entered any information.
Report it to a trusted adult, your bank, or the platform.
Watch your accounts for any strange activity.

habits: Trusting a message just because it looks official.
whyBadExplanations: Scammers are good at copying real companies, school names, and bank alerts.

slides.title: Real Contact vs. Scam Contact
slides.leftBody: Gives you time to verify through official channels. Points to their official website you already know. Does not ask for full passwords or SSN over text. Professional, calm, no threats.
slides.rightBody: Demands you act in minutes or lose access. Sends a link or number you have never seen before. Asks for passwords, SSN, or full card numbers. Threatening, alarming, or suspiciously exciting.

slides.myth: Only older people fall for scams.
slides.truth: Teens and young adults are actually one of the most targeted groups — especially through social media, gaming platforms, and fake job offers. Anyone can be scammed.

slides.myth: If I already sent money, there's nothing I can do.
slides.truth: Act fast. Contact your bank immediately, report it to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov, and notify the platform you used. Some payments can be reversed or flagged.

slides.myth: Scams are obvious — bad grammar, weird logos.
slides.truth: Modern scams can look completely professional. AI-generated messages and cloned websites are getting harder to spot by appearance alone.

slides.title: Financial Scams and Fraud Recap
takeaways: Scammers often use urgency, fear, or excitement.
A message looking real does not mean it is real.
Always verify through an official source you found yourself.
If something feels off, pause and check first.
Anyone can get scammed — acting fast after the fact can reduce the damage.

name: Banking Basics
description: In this lesson you will learn the difference between checking and savings accounts, how overdraft fees work, and how to choose a bank or credit union.
objectives: Checking accounts are for spending and savings accounts are for storing money
Overdraft fees can make small mistakes expensive
Banks and credit unions offer similar services, but their fees and features can differ
Choosing an account should be based on your real needs, not just what sounds familiar

slides.definition: A checking account is used for everyday money. It is the account most people use for debit cards, direct deposit, bill payments, and regular spending.
A savings account is for money you want to keep safe and not spend often. It usually earns more interest than a checking account, but it is not meant for daily swiping and spending.

items.title: Checking
items.description: Best for spending, swiping, paying bills, and getting direct deposit.

items.title: Savings
items.description: Best for emergency money, short-term goals, and money you want to leave alone.

items.title: Daily Use
items.description: Checking is usually the better choice for money you use all the time.

items.title: Protected Money
items.description: Savings works better when you want your money to sit there and grow a little.

slides.question: What is usually the best use for a savings account?
options: Paying for lunch every day with a debit card
Keeping money for emergencies or future goals
Using it to make dozens of purchases every week
Sending money to friends all the time
explanations: That is usually what a checking account is for.
Savings accounts are better for money you want to hold onto.
A savings account is not meant for constant everyday spending.
That is usually done through checking or a payment app connected to checking.

slides.definition: An overdraft happens when you spend more money than you have in your checking account. Some banks cover the purchase and then charge you a fee, which can make a small mistake cost a lot more.

slides.scenario: You have $12 in your checking account. You buy a snack and drink for $15 with your debit card.
slides.question: What would happen?
options: Nothing happens because the bank will cover it for free.
Your card might be declined, or the bank might approve it and charge a fee.
It turns into a savings account purchase automatically.
explanations: Some banks may approve the purchase and then charge an overdraft fee, or it might get declined.
What happens depends on the account settings and the bank, but either way, spending more than you have can cause a problem.
That does not happen automatically unless you set up a specific transfer or protection option.

slides.title: How to Choose a Bank or Credit Union
steps: Check whether there is a monthly fee.
Ask about overdraft fees and minimum balance rules.
Look for ATM access near where you live, work, or go to school.
Compare mobile app quality and online banking tools.
Check whether the account has direct deposit, transfers, and alerts.
Read the fine print before opening the account.

slides.title: Bank or Credit Union?
slides.optionA: Big Bank with lots of branches and ATMs
slides.optionB: Local Credit Union with fewer branches
slides.consequenceA: More convenience in many places, but sometimes higher fees.
slides.consequenceB: Often lower fees and better customer service, but fewer locations.

slides.title: What Is FDIC Insurance — and Why Does It Matter?
slides.prompt: You keep hearing that banks are 'FDIC insured.' What does that actually mean for you?
slides.revealedContent: FDIC insurance means the federal government protects up to $250,000 of your money if a bank fails. Credit unions have equivalent coverage through NCUA. As long as your bank or credit union carries this protection, your money is safe even if the institution goes under. Always confirm before opening an account.

habits: Swiping your card without checking your balance first.
whyBadExplanations: A small purchase can turn into a bigger problem if it causes an overdraft or gets declined at the wrong time.

slides.title: Banking Basics Recap
takeaways: Checking is for everyday spending.
Savings is for money you want to protect and keep.
Overdraft fees can make small mistakes expensive.
FDIC and NCUA insurance protect your money up to $250,000.
Compare fees, access, and account features before choosing where to bank.

name: Digital Money
description: In this lesson you will learn how digital payments work, how to use payment apps more safely, and what risks come with fast online money transfers.
objectives: Digital money is convenient, but fast payments can be hard to reverse
Sending money to the wrong person can be a real problem
Payment apps are useful, but they are not always as protected as a bank
You should always double-check before you tap send

slides.definition: Digital money is money you use electronically instead of with cash. This includes debit card purchases, mobile payment apps, digital wallets, and bank transfers.

items.title: Payment Apps
items.description: Apps like Venmo or Cash App let people send money quickly to other people.

items.title: Digital Wallets
items.description: Digital wallets store payment information on your phone or device so you can pay without using a physical card.

items.title: Wire Transfers
items.description: Wire transfers move money directly from one bank to another, often quickly and sometimes with fees.

items.title: Digital Risks
items.description: Fast payments can also mean scams, wrong transfers, weak passwords, or fake payment requests.

slides.question: What is one big risk of digital payments?
options: They are always safer than cash in every situation.
You can always undo a payment instantly if you change your mind.
They can be sent very quickly to the wrong person or a scammer.
They never need passwords or account protection.
explanations: Digital payments can be safe, but they still come with risks.
Some payments are very hard to reverse once they are sent.
Speed is convenient, but it also means mistakes and scams can happen fast.
Strong passwords and account security matter a lot with digital money.

slides.definition: A digital wallet is a tool on your phone or device that stores your payment information so you can pay online, in apps, or in stores without pulling out a physical card.

slides.title: Fast Tap or Careful Check?
slides.optionA: Send money the second you get a request
slides.optionB: Pause and verify the name, amount, and reason first
slides.consequenceA: Risky. A rushed payment can go to the wrong person or a scammer.
slides.consequenceB: Safer. A quick check can prevent a costly mistake.

slides.scenario: Your friend texts and says, "Can you Venmo me $40 right now?" The username looks close to theirs, but not exactly the same.
slides.question: What is the right move?
options: Send it anyway since the profile picture looks familiar.
Text or call your friend to confirm the exact account first.
Send a smaller amount first and hope it goes to the right person.
explanations: Copying an account is a classic type of scam.
It is smart to verify before sending money.
Even a small payment can still go to the wrong account.

slides.title: How to Use Payment Apps More Safely
steps: Double-check the username before sending money.
Confirm requests with the person another way if anything looks off.
Use strong passwords and turn on two-factor authentication.
Do not keep large amounts of money sitting in a payment app.
Watch out for fake messages about payments, refunds, or account problems.
Review your transaction history often.

habits: Treating payment apps like they are foolproof.
whyBadExplanations: These apps are convenient, but they can still be used for scams, mistakes, and fake payment requests.

slides.title: Is Money in a Payment App Protected Like a Bank?
slides.prompt: You have $200 sitting in your Venmo or Cash App balance. Is it as safe as money in a bank?
slides.revealedContent: No — not in the same way. Payment app balances are generally not FDIC insured unless you have opted into a specific bank-linked feature. If the app has a problem or your account gets compromised, you have fewer protections than you would with a real bank account. The safest move is to transfer money out to your bank account instead of leaving it sitting in the app.

slides.title: Digital Money Recap
takeaways: Digital money makes payments faster and easier.
Fast payments can also make mistakes harder to fix.
Always verify the person, amount, and account before sending money.
Good account security matters when your money is online.
Money left in payment apps may not have the same protections as a bank account.

name: Financial Conversations and Shared Money
description: In this lesson you will learn how to talk about money clearly with other people, how to split costs fairly, and how to avoid confusion when money is shared.
objectives: Money problems often come from unclear expectations, not just lack of money
It is better to talk about costs early than argue about them later
Shared money works better when everyone knows who pays for what
Clear communication can prevent awkwardness, stress, and resentment

slides.definition: Shared money means money situations where more than one person is involved. This can include splitting rent, paying for food together, covering group costs, or helping family members with expenses.

items.title: Roommates
items.description: Roommates may need to split rent, groceries, utilities, or household items.

items.title: Family Costs
items.description: Families may have conversations about bills, support, spending limits, or who pays for what.

items.title: Group Spending
items.description: Friends often share costs for meals, rides, gifts, trips, or event tickets.

items.title: Expectations
items.description: Problems usually happen when people assume instead of asking directly.

slides.question: What is usually the best way to avoid problems with shared money?
options: Just assume everyone has the same idea about what is fair.
Wait until someone gets upset and then talk about it.
Talk clearly about who is paying, how much, and when.
Let one person handle everything and hope it works out.
explanations: People often have very different expectations, and guessing can create conflict.
Waiting usually makes the problem more awkward and harder to fix.
Clear expectations early can prevent confusion and resentment.
That can create stress, unfairness, and missed payments.

slides.title: Talk Early or Later?
slides.optionA: Bring up the money details before the bill is due
slides.optionB: Stay quiet and assume it will work itself out
slides.consequenceA: Better. It may feel awkward for a minute, but it prevents bigger problems later.
slides.consequenceB: Risky. Small misunderstandings can turn into big arguments.

slides.scenario: You and two roommates are moving into an apartment. Everyone agrees to split costs, but no one has talked about groceries, cleaning supplies, or utilities yet.
slides.question: What should you do first?
options: Wait until the first bills show up and deal with it then.
Set up a quick conversation now about what will be shared and how payments will work.
Pay for extra stuff yourself and say nothing.
explanations: Waiting makes it more likely that people will be surprised or annoyed.
It is much easier to make a plan before confusion starts.
It may seem like you're doing a favor but the costs will pile up fast.

slides.title: How to Have a Clear Money Conversation
steps: Say what the cost is and what it is for.
Be specific about who is paying for what.
Agree on how the cost will be split.
Set a deadline for payment if needed.
Put the plan in writing through text or notes so everyone can check it later.
Speak up early if something feels unfair or unclear.

habits: Saying "It's fine" when you actually feel confused or annoyed about money.
whyBadExplanations: Avoiding the conversation in the moment can create bigger tension later.

slides.definition: An expectation is what someone believes will happen or what they think is fair. Shared money problems often happen when people have different expectations and never say them out loud.

slides.scenario: A friend paid for dinner and said "don't worry about it." Two weeks later they bring it up and say you owe them half.
slides.question: What is the lesson here?
options: You should have offered to pay your share even when they said not to.
Unclear expectations around money can create awkward situations even with people you trust.
You should stop going to dinner with that friend.
explanations: Not quite — the real issue is that the expectation was never actually clarified.
Exactly. "Don't worry about it" means different things to different people. A quick check-in prevents this.
That's a bit extreme. The better fix is a clear conversation next time.

slides.title: Financial Conversations and Shared Money Recap
takeaways: Shared money needs clear communication.
Talking early is usually easier than fixing a conflict later.
Be specific about who pays, how much, and when.
Unclear expectations — not just lack of money — cause most shared money problems.
Clear expectations help protect relationships as well as money.

name: International Money and Access
description: In this lesson you will learn how international money works, what remittances and exchange rates are, and why some people face extra barriers when trying to use banks and financial services.
objectives: Sending money across countries can involve fees, delays, and exchange rates
Exchange rates affect how much money actually arrives
Some people can use banks without a Social Security number, but the process may take more work
Access to money systems is not the same for everyone

slides.definition: A remittance is money sent by a person in one country to someone in another country. This is often done to support family members or cover living costs.

items.title: Remittances
items.description: Some families regularly send money to relatives in another country.

items.title: Exchange Rates
items.description: The value of one currency compared to another affects how much money the other person receives.

items.title: Banking Access
items.description: Some people may not have easy access to bank accounts, credit, or ID documents that banks ask for.

items.title: Transfer Costs
items.description: International money transfers can come with fees, delays, or less favorable exchange rates.

slides.question: What is an exchange rate?
options: A fee charged every time you use a debit card
The value of one country's money compared to another country's money
A loan for people moving to another country
A payment app used only outside the U.S.
explanations: That is a different kind of bank fee.
Exchange rates affect how much money is worth when it is converted.
That is not what an exchange rate is.
An exchange rate is about currency value, not a specific app.

slides.title: Send Fast or Check the Total Cost?
slides.optionA: Use the first transfer service you see
slides.optionB: Compare fees, delivery time, and exchange rates first
slides.consequenceA: Risky. You might pay higher fees or get a worse exchange rate.
slides.consequenceB: Better. The person receiving the money may end up with more.

slides.scenario: Your family wants to send money to a relative in another country. One service has a low fee but a weaker exchange rate. Another has a higher fee but a better exchange rate.
slides.question: What should you do?
options: Choose the service with the lowest fee right away.
Compare both the fee and the exchange rate before deciding.
Pick the service that's more well known.
explanations: A low fee doesn't mean you get more money. Make sure you calculate it out!
The best option is the one that leaves the most value after all costs.
Just because it has a bigger name doesn't mean it's the most cost effective option!

slides.definition: An ITIN is an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number. Some people use it instead of an SSN for certain tax and banking purposes. Do some research on your own if you want — we won't go in depth on this.

slides.title: What to Check Before Sending Money Internationally
steps: Check the transfer fee.
Check the exchange rate.
Look at how long the transfer will take.
Make sure the recipient info is correct.
Compare more than one service.
Confirm how much the other person will actually receive.

habits: Looking only at the fee and ignoring the exchange rate.
whyBadExplanations: A lower fee can still lead to a worse deal if the exchange rate is weaker.

slides.definition: Financial access means being able to use basic money services like bank accounts, transfers, cards, and safe places to store money. Some people face extra barriers because of paperwork, language, immigration status, location, or banking rules.

slides.title: What Does 'Unbanked' Mean — and Why Does It Matter?
slides.prompt: Some people are described as 'unbanked.' What does that mean, and why does it affect their financial life?
slides.revealedContent: Unbanked means someone has no bank or credit union account. Without one, it's harder to receive direct deposit, build savings safely, access credit, or send money cheaply. People may be unbanked due to lack of qualifying ID, distrust of banks, language barriers, fees they can't afford, or immigration status. Understanding this helps explain why financial access is not equal for everyone.

slides.title: International Money and Access Recap
takeaways: Remittances are money sent across countries, often to support family.
Exchange rates change how much money is actually worth in another currency.
Fees and exchange rates both matter in international transfers — compare both.
An ITIN can be used instead of an SSN for some banking purposes.
Financial access is easier for some people than others.

name: Financial Mental Health and Spending Psychology
description: In this lesson you will learn how emotions, stress, habits, and past experiences can affect spending, saving, and money decisions.
objectives: Money is emotional, not just mathematical
Stress, fear, and pressure can affect spending choices
Lifestyle inflation can make you feel broke even when you earn more
Not every money habit is really about money

slides.title: Financial Mental Health and Spending Psychology
slides.subtitle: Lesson 9.6

slides.definition: Money anxiety is stress, fear, or constant worry about money. It can show up even when there is no immediate emergency.

items.title: Money Anxiety
items.description: Some people constantly worry about spending, saving, bills, or the future.

items.title: Emotional Spending
items.description: Some people spend money to feel better, calm down, celebrate, or escape stress.

items.title: Lifestyle Inflation
items.description: As income goes up, spending often goes up too, which can make it harder to build savings.

items.title: Financial Trauma
items.description: Past experiences with poverty, instability, debt, or family conflict can affect how someone thinks about money now.

slides.question: What is lifestyle inflation?
options: When prices go up because of inflation
When you stop using a budget
When you start spending more just because you are making more
When you only buy luxury brands
explanations: That is regular inflation in the economy.
That can happen too, but it's not the actual definition.
Lifestyle inflation happens when extra income turns into extra spending instead of extra progress.
Lifestyle inflation can happen with lots of small upgrades too, not just expensive ones.

slides.title: Raise Your Spending or Raise Your Savings?
slides.optionA: Spend every extra dollar as soon as your income goes up
slides.optionB: Increase your savings and goals before increasing your spending
slides.consequenceA: Risky. It can make you feel stuck even though you are earning more.
slides.consequenceB: Better. This helps you make progress instead of just living more expensively.

slides.scenario: You had a rough week, and now you want to buy a bunch of stuff online because "I deserve it."
slides.question: What should you actually do?
options: Buy everything now because treating yourself always fixes stress.
Pause, wait a little, and ask yourself what you are actually feeling before spending.
Keep shopping, but only if there is a sale.
explanations: A purchase might feel good for a moment, but it does not always solve the real problem.
A short pause can help you tell the difference between a real want and a stress reaction.
A sale does not make it a good decision if you were not planning to buy it.

slides.definition: Emotional spending is buying something mainly because of a feeling, not because you truly need it or planned for it.

slides.title: How To Slow Down an Emotional Money Decision
steps: Pause before buying anything unplanned.
Ask yourself what you are feeling.
Check whether this is a need, a want, or a stress response.
Wait before buying if the purchase is not urgent.
Look at your budget or account balance first.
Choose on purpose instead of reacting in the moment.

habits: Using spending as your main way to cope with stress, boredom, or sadness.
whyBadExplanations: It can create a cycle where emotions lead to spending, and spending leads to more stress later.

slides.definition: Financial trauma is the lasting stress or fear that can come from serious money problems or unstable financial experiences in the past.

slides.prompt:
Think of the last unplanned purchase you made. What were you feeling right before you bought it?

Is there a money situation in your life that feels stressful right now? What would make it feel more manageable?

Do you notice any patterns in when or why you spend — boredom, celebration, anxiety?

slides.title: Financial Mental Health and Spending Psychology Recap
takeaways: Money decisions are often influenced by emotions and past experiences.
Emotional spending can feel good in the moment but cause problems later.
Lifestyle inflation can quietly eat up income increases.
Financial trauma is real and can shape how you think about money.
A short pause before unplanned spending can lead to better choices.

name: Using Money with Purpose
description: In this lesson you will learn how to make money choices that match your values, speak up for yourself in money situations, and use money in more intentional ways.
objectives: Money is not just about buying things — it is also about choices and priorities
Negotiating can help you protect your time, effort, and money
Giving is more meaningful when it is thoughtful and realistic
Spending on purpose means your money reflects what matters to you

slides.definition: Intentional spending means using your money in ways that match your real priorities instead of spending automatically, emotionally, or just because other people are doing it.

slides.title: Ways to Use Money on Purpose

items.title: Negotiating
items.description: Asking for better pay, better terms, or a fairer price instead of automatically accepting the first offer.

items.title: Standing Up for Yourself
items.description: Speaking up when a charge is unfair, when someone owes you money, or when a money situation does not feel right.

items.title: Giving
items.description: Giving can include charity, religious giving, helping family, or supporting causes you care about.

items.title: Values
items.description: Your values help you decide what is worth spending on and what is not.

slides.question: What does it mean to use money with purpose?
options: Spend money only on things that are serious and necessary
Spend money in ways that match your priorities and values
Always choose the cheapest option no matter what
Avoid giving money to other people
explanations: Using money with purpose does not mean you can never spend on fun or enjoyment.
Purposeful money use means your choices line up with what actually matters to you.
The cheapest option is not always the best fit for your goals or values.
Giving can absolutely be part of using money with purpose.

slides.title: Automatic Spending or Intentional Choice?
slides.optionA: Buy things mostly because you are bored, pressured, or copying other people
slides.optionB: Spend after thinking about what matters most to you
slides.consequenceA: This can be bad. Your money will disappear without really improving your life.
slides.consequenceB: This is much smarter. Your money starts reflecting your goals, values, and real priorities.

slides.scenario: You did extra work on a project, but the person paying you gives you less than what was discussed.
slides.question: What is the best response?
options: Say nothing because talking about money is awkward.
Politely remind them of the original agreement and ask about the missing amount.
Decide never to work with anyone again.
explanations: Staying quiet may protect the moment, but it does not protect your time or effort.
Speaking clearly and respectfully is always the best first step.
It makes more sense to address the actual problem first, rather than assuming all following experiences will be the same.

slides.title: How to make a more purposeful money choice
steps: Pause before spending.
Ask yourself what this choice says yes to.
Check whether it fits your values, goals, or real needs.
Think about whether you are acting from pressure, habit, or intention.
Decide whether this is worth the money to you.
Spend, save, give, or walk away on purpose.

slides.definition: Negotiation is one of the most important skills you can know. It's a conversation where people try to reach a fair agreement. This can happen with pay, prices, services, deadlines, or shared costs.

slides.title: How to Negotiate Simply and Respectfully
steps: Know what you want and what you think is fair before the conversation starts.
Be direct and calm — state what you are asking for without over-apologizing.
Give a reason if it helps, but keep it short.
Listen to the other person's response before reacting.
Be willing to meet somewhere in the middle if that feels fair.
If they say no, decide whether to accept, push back once more, or walk away — all three are valid options.

habits: Acting like every price, fee, or unfair money situation is something you just have to accept.
whyBadExplanations: Sometimes the better move is to ask questions, push back politely, or ask for a fairer deal.

slides.title: Using Money with Purpose Recap
takeaways: Purposeful money choices match your values and priorities.
Negotiating is a learnable skill — and it protects your time, effort, and money.
Giving should be thoughtful, not automatic or pressured.
Money works better when you use it intentionally instead of reactively.

name: Putting It All Together
description: In this lesson you will connect the main ideas from the course and see how personal finance works as one system.
objectives: Personal finance is connected
One money choice can affect other areas
Good habits work together over time
You do not need perfection to improve

slides.definition: Personal finance is a system where your income, spending, saving, credit, loans, insurance, and future planning all affect each other.

slides.title: The main parts of the system

items.title: Income
items.description: The money coming in starts everything.

items.title: Spending
items.description: Where your money goes affects what happens next.

items.title: Saving
items.description: Savings help with emergencies and future goals.

items.title: Protection
items.description: Credit, insurance, and planning help protect you from bigger problems.

slides.title: Separate topics vs connected system
slides.optionA: Thinking of each money topic by itself
slides.optionB: Seeing money as one connected system
slides.consequenceA: Easier to miss how one bad choice can cause other problems.
slides.consequenceB: Makes it easier to make smarter long-term decisions.

slides.question: Which statement is most accurate?
options: Personal finance is mostly just budgeting
Personal finance is a connected system of money decisions
Personal finance only matters when you are older
explanations: Budgeting matters, but it is only one part of the bigger picture.
Correct. Income, spending, saving, borrowing, and planning all affect one another.
Many money habits start much earlier.

slides.scenario: A person earns good money, but they spend too much, save nothing, and take on too much debt.
slides.question: What does this show?
options: Income alone solves everything
Personal finance is connected, and one weak area can cause other problems
Saving does not really matter if you have a job
explanations: Good income helps, but it does not fix bad money habits by itself.
Strong income can still be undone by weak spending and saving habits.
Saving still matters because jobs and income can change.

slides.title: A simple way to think about money decisions
steps: Earn money
Decide where it goes
Save some of it
Protect yourself from risk
Plan for future goals

contexts.text: Each link represents one area: income, spending, saving, credit, insurance, planning. Weaken one link and the whole chain feels it.
contexts.label: All connected

contexts.text: Strengthen one area and it often helps the others too — saving more makes debt less necessary, which frees up more income.
contexts.label: Improvement compounds

slides.title: Putting it All Together Recap
takeaways: Personal finance is connected.
One choice affects others.
Good habits work together.
Improvement matters more than perfection.

name: Setting Financial Goals
description: In this lesson, you'll learn how to set financial goals that are clear, realistic, and useful.
objectives: Good financial goals are specific
Goals can be short-term, medium-term, or long-term
A goal should connect to action
Clear goals make better money choices easier

slides.definition: A financial goal is a money target you want to reach, such as saving for something, paying something off, or building more stability.

items.title: Short-term
items.description: Goals for the next days, weeks, or months.

items.title: Medium-term
items.description: Goals for the next year or next few years.

items.title: Long-term
items.description: Goals that may take many years to reach.

items.title: Clear
items.description: The best goals are specific, not vague.

slides.title: Making a good goal
steps: Make it measurable. Set an amount that you want to save, a quota you want to hit, etc.
Make it within a certain time. If there's no deadline, you won't be motivated.
Make it specific. Don't just say you want to make money, say how much you want!

slides.title: What Is an Emergency Fund — and Is That a Goal?
slides.prompt: You keep hearing about emergency funds. Is that the same as a financial goal?
slides.revealedContent: Yes — and it's one of the most important ones to set first. An emergency fund is money saved specifically so that an unexpected expense (car repair, medical bill, lost job) doesn't send you into debt. Most financial advice recommends starting with a goal of $500–$1,000, then building toward 3–6 months of living expenses over time. Set it as a concrete, measurable goal just like any other.

name: Avoiding Common Mistakes
description: In this lesson, you'll review some of the most common money mistakes and how to avoid them.
objectives: Many money problems are predictable
Small bad habits can grow into bigger problems
Awareness helps you avoid expensive mistakes
Prevention is easier than fixing damage later

items.title: Overspending
items.description: Spending too freely can lead to debt fast.

items.title: Not saving
items.description: No savings makes surprises much harder to handle.

items.title: Ignoring details
items.description: Not reading agreements can cost you later.

items.title: Lifestyle inflation
items.description: Spending more every time income rises can keep you stuck.

slides.definition: Lifestyle inflation means raising your spending every time your income goes up, instead of using some of that extra money to save, invest, or build more stability. As you grow you're sure to earn raises, but avoiding keeping your money proportional to your job rather than what's good for you can hurt you.

slides.title: Strong habit vs risky habit
slides.optionA: Reading details, saving something, and pausing before big choices
slides.optionB: Acting fast, spending freely, and ignoring fine print
slides.consequenceA: Lower chance of avoidable mistakes.
slides.consequenceB: Higher chance of expensive problems.

slides.question: Which is an example of lifestyle inflation?
options: Getting a raise and saving part of it
Getting a raise and quickly raising all your spending too
Reading a contract before signing
explanations: That's a strong financial habit to have.
Correct. That is what lifestyle inflation looks like.
That's a smart habit, not a mistake.

slides.question: A student gets their first steady paycheck and starts spending almost all of it because "I'm making money now anyway." What lesson fits best?
options: Spending tends to rise if you do not set limits
Making money does not automatically mean you are building stability
Saving some money early can make future decisions easier
explanations: Correct. This is a common trap when income first starts coming in.
Correct. Income helps, but habits still matter.
Correct. Even a small habit early can make a big difference later.

slides.title: How to avoid common money mistakes
steps: Pause before major spending.
Read agreements before saying yes.
Save some money regularly.
Be careful with debt.
Review your habits once in a while.

slides.question: What is one reason common money mistakes are dangerous?
options: They can slowly become bigger problems over time
They only matter if you are already wealthy
They always get fixed on their own
explanations: Correct. Small bad habits often grow quietly before people notice.
They matter at any income level.
Problems usually grow if ignored.

slides.myth: I'll start saving when I make more money.
slides.truth: People who wait until they earn more usually find a way to spend more too. Starting small now — even $5 a week — builds the habit that actually matters.

slides.myth: I'm young, so money mistakes don't really matter yet.
slides.truth: The habits you build now tend to stick. A bad credit decision at 19 can affect you at 25. A good savings habit at 17 can compound for decades.

slides.myth: I don't need to read the fine print — it's all basically the same.
slides.truth: Fine print is where fees, interest rates, and penalties live. One missed detail in a phone contract, loan agreement, or subscription can cost real money.

slides.title: Avoiding Common Mistakes Recap
takeaways: Many mistakes are predictable.
Small habits matter — good ones compound, bad ones do too.
Awareness helps prevent damage.
Prevention is easier than cleanup.
